blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

I came to this by way of a single sentence, read late at night and not believed at first: that there were people who held the human face to be not a symbol of scripture but scripture itself. Not a metaphor a poet reaches for. The actual text. Ink and page.

The doctrine is real. Fazlallah Astarabadi was born in the city we now call Gorgan around 1340, had a vision in Tabriz in the fasting month of 1374, wrote the Book of Eternity in his own provincial dialect, and had his head taken off at a mountain fortress twenty years later. His greatest poet was flayed alive in Aleppo. A rebel of the movement was skinned in Isfahan. In 1441 some five hundred of them were burned in Tabriz, and among them was Fazlallah's daughter, who had preserved her father's book by copying it out by hand.
I did not have to invent the pattern. It is simply there in the record: a people who said the face is the writing of God, and a world that answered them, over and over, by removing faces.

What drew me was not the persecution. It was the arithmetic. Seven lines issued at birth to every child on earth, seven more arriving with the beard, and among those second seven — the hair in each nostril. A doctrine of beauty would have taken the jaw, the eye, the bow of the lip. This one took nostril hair, because it was not looking at faces the way we look at faces. It was looking for marks. For places where the body reliably lays down a stroke of dark against pale.

It was never about looks. And yet within one generation the poets had it, and were finding the seven verses of the opening chapter in the face of the beloved, and the beloved is always beautiful. That gap — between a doctrine of legibility and a culture that will only ever read the well-printed ones — is the whole of this book.

The rest followed from a question I could not put down. If the face is the writing, then what is a surgeon? We live in the century in which the human face became editable, at scale, cheaply, and largely for the young. Iran performs more of these operations per head than almost anywhere on earth, and the tape across the bridge of the nose is worn openly, sometimes by people who have not had the operation at all. A doctrine that says the face is a divine manuscript has to say something about that. And when I worked out what it would have to say — that a letter added by a man in good faith cannot be told from a letter written by God, because the founder himself established exactly that about four letters of the Persian alphabet — the book stopped being a book about a strange sect and started being a book about my own century.

The body is the last honest witness. That is the line I keep returning to in these publications, and it is not quite true, and this novella is the argument against it. The body does not lie, but it can be written on, and we have got very good at writing on it, and there is no instrument anywhere in creation that reads back the difference.

This is a book about a man who spends his life reading and never once asks whether the page was authored. I do not think he is unusual. I think he is most of us, most of the time, with a better vocabulary.

Grief runs underneath all of it, and I have not tidied it. Sanam is ill from the fifth chapter to the last and she is never cured and she is never ennobled by it. Her illness does not hurt her and it does not make her wise. It simply takes, on one side, patiently, for fourteen months, while the people who love her hold a scholarly disagreement about what she means.
I have left the ending where it belongs, which is with you.
Chew Z
PART ONE — THE SCALP LINE
the first maternal line, from Eve
Here is how you read a dying man.

You do not stand at the foot of the bed. The foot of the bed is where doctors stand, and doctors read a different document. You bring a chair to the right side, close enough that your knees touch the frame, and you sit so that his face and your face are at the same height, because a text held above you is a text you will flatter and a text held below you is a text you will condescend to. Level. Always level. Ostad Rafi'i [os-TAAD ra-fee-EE] — ostad is what you call your teacher in this country, and there is no good English for it; it means the man who taught you your trade and to whom you will never stop owing it — Ostad Rafi'i used to put a folded coat under me when I was a boy because my legs were short and the beds in this city are high.

You wait for the family to stop talking. They never stop on their own. Someone has to say the first words of the Fatiha [FAA-teh-heh] — the opening chapter of the Qur'an, seven verses, and there is a reason we begin there that I will come to — and then the room goes quiet the way a room goes quiet when a needle is set on a record.
Then you look at his hairline.

Not his eyes. Everyone looks at the eyes and the eyes are not writing, they are only wet. The hairline is writing. It is the first of the lines, the highest stroke on the page, and in a man of eighty-one it will have retreated and thinned and forked and gone grey in a pattern that is his and no one else's on this earth, and that pattern is a letter, and the letter has a value, and the value has a meaning, and the meaning is what you have come to say aloud in front of his children.

That night in Kordkuy [kord-KOO-ee] the man was named Hasan Dastgheib [ha-SAN dast-GHAYB] and he had four days left, though nobody had told him and he had told everybody. His hairline had gone back to the crown on the left and stopped dead on the right, an unequal retreat, a shoreline where the sea had taken one bay and left the other. I read it as ha [HAA]. Eight. The letter that opens his own name and also opens the word for truth, and I said so, and his daughter put the back of her hand against her mouth.
That is the whole trade. That is what I do and what my father did and what his mother did before him.
A word about what we are, since you will want to know and since nobody has ever said it plainly in print.

We are Hurufis [hoo-ROO-feez]. Huruf [hoo-ROOF] is Arabic for letters — the letters of the alphabet — and a Hurufi is a person who believes the alphabet is not a tool for describing God but the substance God is made of. Twenty-eight letters in Arabic. Thirty-two in Persian. Everything that exists was spoken into existing, and a spoken thing is made of sounds, and sounds are made of letters, and therefore the whole created world, the mountains and the Caspian and the mould on the north wall of my kitchen, is text.
And the human face is the page where the text is largest.

Not like a page. This is the part where people nod politely and go away having misunderstood, so let me stop and put my hand flat on the table. Poets have been saying for a thousand years that the beloved's face is like a book, that her brows are like the letter nun, that her mouth is like a mim. That is decoration. That is a man reaching for something pretty to say to a girl in a courtyard.
We do not mean like.

We mean that if you had been present at the beginning and had asked to see the writing, you would have been shown a face. We mean that the lines on your father's forehead are not evidence of a text, they are the text, they are ink, and when he dies the ink dries and no one will ever read that particular sentence again in the history of the world. We mean that scripture is not kept in mosques. It is kept in houses, it is kept in prisons, it is kept in the beds of hospitals in provincial cities, and it walks around all day being ignored by everyone including itself.

Six hundred years ago there were tens of thousands of us. There was a rebellion. There were several. In this city, in this province, in the fifteenth century, there were enough of us that the men with the fatwas had to sit down and do arithmetic about how many they would need to burn.
Now there are three families.

I drove home from Kordkuy at one in the morning with the heater failing and the fog coming up off the flats the way it does here, thick and low and the colour of unwashed wool, so that the road appears one dashed white line at a time and you take it on faith that the line will keep being offered. I have driven that road four hundred times. I have driven it after readings that broke me open and after readings that were nothing, a tired old page, a life that had said very little and said it clearly.
Sanam had left the kitchen light on.

She was asleep at the table with her cheek on her forearm and the ledger open, because she kept the ledger, the who-died-and-when-and-what-was-said, in a hand so small and even that Tuba Khanum once held a page up to the window and said it was the only handwriting in the lineage that looked like it had been printed by a machine that loved you.
I stood in the doorway with my coat on and I read my wife's face for the four thousandth time.

The scalp line, high and unbroken, no retreat at all at forty-four, a full clean stroke from temple to temple like the top rule of a page. The brows heavy and level. The lashes — four sets, upper and lower, right and left — dark and thick enough that she never wore anything on them and never had.
Seven lines. Not fourteen. She would never have fourteen. No woman ever has.

I will explain that. It is the ugliest thing in the doctrine and I am not going to hide it from you, but not yet, because at that moment I was not thinking about doctrine. I was thinking that she had left the light on for me and fallen asleep under it, and that in twenty-four years I had never once come home to a dark house.
I woke her badly and she said a name that was not mine, some dream, and then she laughed and put her hand over her eyes.
Ten weeks later that hand would not be able to close.
Tuba Khanum brought me the girl on a Thursday, in the rain, without warning, which is how Tuba Khanum has done everything for the fifty years I have known her.
"Golnaz Ehsani [gol-NAAZ eh-saa-NEE]," she said. "Nineteen. She reads better than you did at nineteen."
"Everyone read better than I did at nineteen."
"Yes," said Tuba Khanum, and sat down and took the good chair.

The girl stood in the hall with rain in her hair and her shoes still on, which no one in this country does, and I understood immediately that she was frightened and had decided to be rude instead. Her face was — I am going to be careful here, because of what comes later, and because I want you to see exactly what I saw and exactly what I did not.
Her face was a clean copy. That is the phrase we use and I want to explain it before it starts doing damage.

We do not say beautiful. We are the only people in the world who look at faces professionally and have no word for beautiful, and this confuses everyone, and the confusion has killed people. What we say is legible [in Persian, khwana [khaa-NAA], readable]. A legible face is one where the fourteen lines — or in a woman the seven — are distinct from each other and from the ground, where the brow does not run into the lash and the lash does not run into the shadow, where a reader coming to it cold can say with confidence this is where this line begins and this is where it ends.
That is a property of contrast and edge. It has nothing to do with proportion. It has nothing to do with whether the arrangement pleases you.

You can have a face that would stop traffic and read like water. You can have a face that makes children go quiet — a burn, a palsy, a jaw carried wrong since birth — and every line on it can be so sharp and so separate that reading it is like being handed a book with the pages cut for you.
So: her face was a clean copy. Sharp brow, sharp lash, high contrast, easy ground. I could have read her across a room in bad light.

I did not know then that this was because a woman I had not yet met had made her that way with a blade, in a room off the ring road, for eleven million tomans, when Golnaz was seventeen and had begged her mother for a year.

I want to be fair to myself. There was no way to know. That is the entire problem and it will be the entire problem for the rest of this book: there is no way to know. Fazlallah himself, six hundred years dead, wrote the sentence that makes it unknowable, and he wrote it thinking he was closing a hole, and instead he opened the one I fell through.
But that is chapter twenty-nine. On the Thursday, in the rain, I only thought: good, this will be easy, I am tired, let it be easy.
"Take your shoes off," I said.
She took them off.
"What did you see first?"
"Your wife," she said. "In the kitchen. She looked at me."
"That is not what I asked."
"You asked what I saw first."
Tuba Khanum, from the good chair, made a small sound like a kettle deciding.

I took the girl into the back room where my father read and his mother read, and I sat her at the table under the north window, which is the only light in this house that does not lie, and I gave her the first lesson, which has been the first lesson since before Persia had a Persian alphabet.
"There are seven lines that you have had since you were born," I said. "Name them."
"The hair on my head. Both eyebrows. Four sets of lashes — upper and lower, each eye."

"That is seven. They are called khutut-e ummiya [kho-TOOT-eh om-MEE-yeh]. The maternal lines. Ummiya from umm [OOM], mother. The doctrine holds that they descend to you from Eve, and that every child born anywhere on earth arrives with all seven, and that no other feature on the human body is issued so completely and so early."
"And the other seven?"

I did not answer that for a moment, because through the wall I could hear Sanam running the tap, and because the honest answer to that question is the reason this doctrine has never spread and never will.
"The other seven," I said, "arrive with the beard."
PART TWO — THE RIGHT BROW

The other seven are called khutut-e abiya [kho-TOOT-eh a-BEE-yeh]. The paternal lines. From ab [AB], father. They descend from Adam and they arrive at puberty and here they are, all seven, and I want you to hear them in order because the order is the point:

The hair down the right side of the face. The hair down the left side of the face. The right half of the moustache. The left half of the moustache. The hair in the right nostril. The hair in the left nostril. The tuft between the lower lip and the chin.
Read that list again.
Nostril hair.

I have watched this land on perhaps thirty people in my life, initiates and outsiders both, and it lands the same way every time: a pause, and then a small movement of the mouth that the person tries to suppress. They think they have caught us being ridiculous. They are about to be polite about it.
What they have actually caught is the only honest thing in the entire system.

Because think about what a doctrine of beauty would have done with those seven slots. It would have taken the line of the jaw. It would have taken the shape of the eye, the bridge of the nose, the bow of the upper lip — it would have taken exactly the seven things that every love poem in this language has been taking for a thousand years. That is what a doctrine of beauty looks like. We know what one looks like. We are surrounded by one.
Fazlallah took nostril hair.

He took it because he was not looking at faces the way you look at faces. He was looking for marks. For places where the body reliably grows hair — everywhere, on everyone, without being asked — and so lays down a stroke of dark against pale. A line. An inking. And the nose reliably does that, in every man of every people, and so it is in, and the jaw is out, because the jaw is a shape and shapes are not letters.
This is the single fact that I would put on the wall of every room where our doctrine is discussed, and I would put it there in a large hand:
It was never about looks.
It was about whether a line is present and whether you can see where it stops.
Now the arithmetic, and I will go slowly, because the arithmetic is what makes the doctrine a doctrine rather than a hobby.

Seven maternal and seven paternal is fourteen. Fourteen matters for a reason outside the face: there are twenty-nine chapters of the Qur'an that open with letters standing alone, letters that spell no word, that sit at the top of the page saying nothing — alif lam mim, ta ha, ya sin. Every commentator for eight hundred years had filed them under the obscure verses, the ones whose meaning God has kept. Fazlallah moved them to the clear ones. And when you strip out the repeats, those disconnected letters number exactly fourteen.

Fourteen letters that mean nothing on the page. Fourteen lines that mean nothing on the face. He put them together and said: they are the same fourteen, and neither of them is silent, and the reason you cannot read them at the top of the chapter is that you have been reading in the wrong place. Go and look in a mirror.
Fourteen doubled is twenty-eight, which is the Arabic alphabet entire.
Then four more, which is the part I will need you to remember in a year's time when a woman in a white coat says it back to me in a consulting room and I have nothing to answer her with.

Persian has thirty-two letters. Arabic has twenty-eight. The four extra ones — pe, che, zhe, gaf — exist because Persian has four sounds that Arabic does not, and scribes centuries after the Prophet took existing Arabic letters and added dots to them and made new ones. That is the historical account. That is what any philologist will tell you and any philologist is right.
Fazlallah denied it.

Not the history — he was not a stupid man, he could see the dots. He denied the conclusion. He held that the thirty-two are the thirty-two pre-eternal words, the names taught to Adam before there was time, and that when those scribes sat down and improvised four letters they were not inventing anything. They were remembering. Their hands were being run. The four that look added are not added; they were always there and merely arrived late, and there is no test, no instrument, no reading anywhere in the world that can distinguish a letter God wrote from a letter a man added in good faith.
And to prove it he pointed at the mouth: thirty-two teeth. Not twenty-eight. God did not put twenty-eight teeth in your head and then let the Persians add four.
I taught Golnaz that on her third day and she said, "So the fake ones are real."
"There are no fake ones. That is what it means."
"That is not what it means," she said. "It means you can't tell."
I remember laughing. I remember thinking, this one is going to be difficult, and being pleased about it, the way you are pleased when a student is going to cost you something.

Sanam came in with tea while we were on the thirty-two and stayed to listen, standing, one hip against the doorframe, because she had heard it four hundred times and liked it anyway, the way you like a song you have worn out.
"Ask him the woman question," she said to Golnaz.
Golnaz looked at me.
"Ask it," I said.
"Women only have seven."
"Yes."
"Forever."
"Yes."
"So a woman is half a text."
Sanam said, without any particular heat, in the voice she used for the neighbours: "A woman is half a text, and it will be a man who tells you what the half says."

Then she put the tray down and went out and I heard her in the kitchen turn the radio on, and Golnaz sat there with her hands flat on the table and did not ask me anything else for the rest of the afternoon.

I want to record that I did not defend the doctrine at that moment. I have gone over it many times since. I had the defence ready — I have always had it ready, it is the standard one, that the maternal seven are the older and purer set, that Eve's letters were given before Adam's were earned, that in the reading of the dying it is almost always the maternal lines that carry the sentence and the paternal that carry the ornament. All of that is in the books. All of it is arguable. Some of it I still think is true.
I said nothing, because my wife had walked out of the room, and because in twenty-four years I had learned that the argument was not one I could win in the kitchen.
Eight days later she woke up and the right side of her mouth would not come with her.
THE FIRST RECITATION

Delivered at the house of Tuba Khanum, on the fourth night of the month in which he died, before the households of the three families and two children who were too young for it, as it has been delivered in this province for six hundred years.
He was a merchant's son from this city.

Not from Tabriz, not from Isfahan, not from any of the places where a man is supposed to become a prophet. From here. From Astarabad [as-taa-raa-BAAD]. That is the old name of the city you are sitting in. The maps say Gorgan [gor-GAAN] now, and have said Gorgan since your grandmother was a girl, and that is the whole reason nobody outside these three families connects the founder of our doctrine with the town where they buy their bread.
His name was Fazlallah [fazl-ol-LAAH]. It means the generosity of God. He was born around the year the plague came the second time, into money, and he was expected to take the business.

He did not take the business. He was one of those young men — you have met one, every generation has one — who reads Rumi at fourteen and is ruined by it. He went out to the dervishes — the wandering poor men of the Sufi orders, who own one bag and no house and are fed by strangers. He gave things away. And what he was chiefly known for in those years was not preaching, because he did not preach yet, but dreams: his own and other people's. People brought him their dreams the way you bring a doctor a cough. He became, in his twenties, the best-regarded interpreter of dreams in the northeast of this country, and he was still nobody, and he would have died nobody.
In Tabriz, in the fasting month, in the year that we count as 1374 in the calendar the foreigners use, he stopped being nobody.

He called what happened to him zuhur-e kebriya [zo-HOOR-eh keb-ree-YAA]. The manifestation of glory. He never described the event itself. Six hundred years of us and we do not know what he saw, whether it came at night or in the afternoon, whether he was alone. He described only what he was given, and what he was given was a key: that the letters standing silent at the heads of twenty-nine chapters were not silent, were not obscure, were not held back — that they were the clearest verses in the book, and that the reason no one could read them was that everyone had been looking at paper.
And then he did the thing that makes him ours rather than one more ecstatic with a following.
He wrote it down.

He wrote the Javdan-nama [jaa-vee-DAAN naa-MEH], the Book of Eternity, and he wrote it in the dialect of this province, in the language of this valley, in words that a Tabrizi could barely follow and a Baghdadi could not follow at all. Scholars have called this a mistake for six centuries. It was not a mistake. He was saying: the revelation is local. It is in the mouth you already have. You do not have to go anywhere.

You do not have to go to Mecca. You do not have to go to Karbala [kar-ba-LAA], where the grandson of the Prophet was killed and where half this country would go tomorrow if it could. You do not have to cross a single river.

The alphabet is already on you. It came with the body. It was issued at birth, seven lines of it, and topped up at fifteen, and it has been sitting on the front of your head your whole life being looked at by everyone you have ever met and read by no one.
That is what the man from this city said.
They took his head off for it twenty years later and we will come to that.
Here the recitation ends, and the tea is brought, and no one speaks for the length of time it takes to pour eleven glasses.
PART THREE — THE LEFT BROW
It started with a drinking glass.

She was holding it in her right hand at half past six in the morning and the water came out of the right side of her mouth and went down her chin and onto her front, and she said a word I had heard her say perhaps four times in twenty-four years, and put the glass down, and pressed the back of her wrist against her lips, and looked at me.
"Say something," she said.
"You said something."
"No. You say something. I want to see if I can smile."

She could not smile. Half of her could. The right side of her face had come off the rope. The corner of the mouth, the fold beside the nose, the whole business a face uses to say I am joking — gone, on that side, in the night, without a sound, while I slept next to her.
And the eye.
The right eye would not close.

That is the thing nobody warns you about, because everyone imagines the slack mouth and nobody imagines the eye. She would blink and the left lid would come down and the right would come down halfway and stop, and the eye would sit there, wet, exposed, looking at me out of a face that was doing something else entirely.
We drove to the hospital in Gorgan in the dark with the heater failing.
The doctor was about thirty and very tired and very kind and she said the word to us within four minutes.

I am not going to write the word down. Not now and not later. In this book you will get the slack side, the sword-cut, the hollowing, the thinning ground — you will get what a reader sees, because a reader is what I am, and because the names doctors use are a different alphabet with a different god and I refuse to hand my wife over to it in a book that is about her face.
But the thirty-year-old doctor said the word, and then she said the thing that we held onto for eleven weeks like a rope in water:
"Most people get most of it back. Six weeks. Sometimes ten."

She put Sanam on steroids and gave her eye drops for the eye that would not close and a small clear patch to tape it shut at night, and she said the word idiopathic, which I did look up, and which turns out to mean: this happens and we do not know why.
I want to be exact about what I felt in that room, because I have been dishonest about it in my own head for a long time and this is where I stop.
I felt fear. Of course.

And underneath the fear, in the same second, moving fast and low like something under ice, I felt: the right brow has dropped four millimetres and the lash line has changed angle and I do not know what it says now.

I would like to tell you that I was ashamed of that. I was not ashamed of it for another five months. At the time it seemed to me the most natural thing in the world, in the way that a doctor whose wife falls ill notices her colour before he notices his own heart.
That is what I told myself.
It is not the same. A doctor's noticing is in service of the woman. Mine was already in service of something else.
She was very good about it for eleven weeks.

She taped the eye at night and made a joke about the tape. She learned to drink from the left corner. She got a straw and then decided the straw was undignified and went back to the glass and simply turned her head, and told the neighbours she had slept in a draught, which is what everyone in this country says, and everyone in this country accepts it.
She would not let me read her.
I asked once, in the second week, in what I thought was a light voice, and she said, "No," and went on peeling an orange with one hand and her teeth.
"It might—"
"Mansur. No."
"You have never once said no."
"I have never once been a text you wanted to read," she said. "You have read me the way a man reads the back of a cereal box. Now I am interesting. No."
I did not have an answer to that. I have not found one since.
At week eleven the doctor said, "Hm," and stopped writing.

The mouth had come back about a third of the way. The eye was closing to perhaps three-quarters. And that, apparently, is not the shape of the curve. The curve is supposed to be a bad month and then a rising line and then, one morning, an unremarkable face doing unremarkable things. It is not supposed to be a third and then a plateau and then, on the right temple, a groove.
The groove was new that week. Neither of us had mentioned it because each of us had decided the other had not seen it.

She had them run the scans. It took until the end of the month to get a slot and eleven days after that to get the reading, and in those eleven days I did something I had never done in my life, which is that I lied to Tuba Khanum. She asked how Sanam was and I said improving.
I want to explain why I lied, because it was not to protect Sanam.
It was because our doctrine has no provision for what was happening.
Let me lay this out plainly, because everything after this follows from it, and if I do not get it into your hands now then nothing I do later will make any sense.
We read faces. A face is scripture. Very well. Now: what do you do with a bad face?

We have an answer for that, and it is a good answer, and it is six hundred years old. A face with poor contrast, a face where the ground is thick and the lines blur into it, a face obscured by fat or by scar or by an unlucky arrangement of bone — that is a hard manuscript. A cramped hand. Bad ink, thin paper, a scribe in a hurry. The text is not wrong. The text is hard to read, which is a fact about you and your light and your patience, and not a fact about God. You sit closer. You wait for better light. You come back tomorrow. Nobody in six hundred years has ever suggested that an ugly man is heresy.

And we have an answer for a false face, which is the great crime and which I will get to, and which I did not think about once in those eleven days because it did not occur to me that it could have anything to do with my wife.
But a face that is changing?
A face where the lines were one thing on Tuesday and are another thing by Friday, and will be a third thing by Ramadan?

There is nothing. I have read the Javdan-nama in the poor Persian summary and in as much of the valley dialect as I can manage. I have read Firishteoglu [fee-rish-teh-OH-loo], the man who put the whole thing into Turkish sixty years after the founder died, and whose version my father made me learn for exactly this reason. I have been through every commentary that the three families hold, and we hold a great many, because when you are the last of something you keep everything.
There is nothing on a text that revises itself.
Six hundred years of men who believed the face was God's handwriting, and not one of them wrote down what to do when the handwriting moves.
You see the shape of the hole. I saw it at the time and I told myself I was seeing a scholarly gap, an unaddressed case, a footnote for the lineage.
Here is what was actually in the hole, and I was not able to look at it for another year:
If the face is God's writing — then whatever changes the face is God writing.
Not permitting. Not testing. Not punishing.
Writing.

Which means the thing eating my wife's face was not an interruption of the scripture. It was the scripture continuing. It was the pen still moving. And every prayer I might make for her recovery — every single one, in any language, at any hour — was a request that God stop writing and put back what He had crossed out.

I did not think that thought in week eleven. I want to be accurate. In week eleven I stood in a corridor and lied to a seventy-one-year-old woman about my wife's recovery, and told myself it was kindness, and drove home, and did not turn on the light in the kitchen because Sanam was asleep, and stood in the dark for a while, and went to bed.

But the thought was already in the house. It had come in with the tape on her eye. It sat in the corner of every room I was in for the next fourteen months, and it was patient, and it did not need me to look at it, because it knew perfectly well that I would.
PART FOUR — THE UPPER RIGHT LASHES
The groove came down her forehead over about nine weeks, and by the end of the winter you could lay a matchstick in it.

It ran from just inside the hairline, a little right of the middle, down past the inner end of the right eyebrow, and stopped. It was not a wrinkle. A wrinkle is a fold and folds have a fat side and a thin side and they move when you move. This did not move. It was a line where the ground had gone from underneath the skin, so that the skin lay down into the place where something used to be, and it was pale, and it had a clean edge on both sides, and it did not go away when she raised her brows or slept or cried.

They have a name for it in the hospital. They call it a sword-cut, which is the only honest thing the other alphabet has ever said about this illness, and I have used their name ever since because it is better than mine would have been.
Here is what it is, in my words, since I promised you my words.

The ground under her face was thinning. Not the skin — the padding, the quiet fat and the sheet of muscle and, eventually, the bone itself, on the right side only, in a slow drift downward and outward from that first line. It does not hurt. That is the part people cannot hold in their heads. It never once hurt her. It simply took, at a rate you could not see by looking but could see by photographs eight weeks apart, and it took only from the right, and it stopped exactly at the middle of her face as though something had drawn a border and honoured it.
The middle of the face. Where the border ran.
I need to tell you about the middle of the face and I need you to forgive me for how this is going to sound.

There is a line down the centre of every human face. Down the brow, down the ridge of the nose, through the notch of the lip, over the chin. It is not one of the fourteen. It is not a letter at all. In our books it is called the khatt-e istiva [khat-teh es-tee-VAA] — the line of settling — and the word comes out of the Qur'an, out of the verse that says of God that He settled upon the throne, istawa [es-ta-VAA], and which Fazlallah read as meaning that the throne is the form of Adam and the settling is the fact of the face.
The line of settling is where God sits.
Not a letter. The place from which the letters are read. The spine of the page, the fold, the axis the whole document is hung on.

And in the first week of that spring, with the light coming back and the fog off the flats in the mornings, my wife's illness opened a clean vertical stroke down the top of the line of settling and then began, from that stroke, to take the right-hand page.

There is a letter that looks exactly like that stroke. Alif [a-LEEF]. The first letter. A single vertical mark, no curve, no dot, nothing to decorate it, and its value in the counting is one, and it is the letter that stands for unity, for the one, for the beginning of the alphabet and the beginning of everything the alphabet was used to say.
You draw it by putting the pen down at the top and pulling straight down and lifting.
It is the mark a scribe makes first when he is testing a new pen.
I did not say any of this to her.
I said none of it to Tuba Khanum either, or to Golnaz, who came twice a week and had begun to arrive with food her mother had cooked, which is what this city does instead of asking.
I said it to a notebook.

I bought the notebook in a stationer's near the bazaar on a Tuesday, and I remember standing in the shop for a long time choosing between two of them, one with a soft cover and one with a hard one, and thinking about which would survive better, and only realising on the pavement outside what that thought had been for.
You do not choose a durable notebook for a private grief.
You choose a durable notebook for a record.
THE SECOND RECITATION
Delivered at the house of Tuba Khanum, on the sixth night, before the same room, one of the children having been kept home with a fever.
He tried to convert Timur.

That is the sentence that ends the first part of our history and every one of us has heard it since we were four years old, and I have never once heard it said with anything but a kind of exhausted love, the way a family talks about the uncle who put the money into the wrong bank.

Understand what he was doing. He had a doctrine that said the divine is on your face and the pilgrimage is unnecessary and the letters are the substance of the world, and he had it in a book, and he had perhaps a few thousand followers in Isfahan and Khorasan [kho-raa-SAAN] and Shirvan [sheer-VAAN] and Baku, and he looked around at the fourteenth century and made a perfectly rational decision: convert the man with the army.
He wrote to Timur [tee-MOOR] — the conqueror the Europeans call Tamerlane, who at that moment owned everything between here and India. He made overtures. He wanted an audience.
You may imagine the letter. We do not have it.
What we have is what Timur's son did about it.

The son's name was Miranshah [mee-raan-SHAAH]. He was the governor of Azerbaijan and by every account including his own family's he was going mad in those years, and he took Fazlallah at a fortress called Alinja [a-leen-JAA], in Nakhchivan [nakh-chee-VAAN], up in the mountains of the far northwest, in the year 1394.
He had him beheaded.
Now.

I am going to stop the recitation here, as my father stopped it, as his mother stopped it, and say the thing that we say at this point in the story and that we have never once written down, because it is the reason we recite this at all rather than simply reading it out of a history.
Fazlallah taught that the face is the throne of God and the whole scripture of creation.
And the punishment that was chosen for him, out of all the punishments available in that century — and there were many, and Miranshah knew them — was the one that takes the face off the body.
Nobody planned that. Miranshah was not making a point about doctrine. He was a violent man in a violent province and it was the ordinary sentence.
But it happened. It is the first time it happened.

It is not the last time it happened, and when we recite in two nights' time you will hear it happen again, and in four nights' time you will hear it again, and the last time you hear it, it will not be a face that is taken but a whole roomful of them at once, and one of them will be his daughter's.
We are a people whose founder said the face is the writing of God, and every time the world has answered us, it has answered by removing faces.

The grave at Alinja became a place of pilgrimage. They went there in the month he died. They wore the white cloth that pilgrims wear to Mecca and they walked around his tomb seven times and then seven times again, and if you have been listening to anything I have said in this room you know why it was seven and then seven, and you know that they were not walking around a tomb.
They were reading him.

Seven for the lines his mother gave him. Seven for the lines his father gave him. Around and around a dead man in the snow in Nakhchivan, with the Kaaba behind them and forgotten — the black cube at Mecca, the house every Muslim on earth turns to five times a day — because a house is only ever a picture of a face.
Here the recitation ends. Tea is brought. Tonight it was
Sanam Sarmadi who poured, with her left hand, from the doorway, and did not sit down.
PART FIVE — THE LOWER RIGHT LASHES
I read her for the first time on a Thursday night in the fourth month, while she slept.

I want to describe this properly, because I have found that people assume it was furtive and quick, a man leaning over a bed in the dark, and it was not that. It was worse than that. It took two hours and I set it up like a job.

She slept on her left side, which put the right of her face upward, which was convenient, and I have thought about that word since. I moved the reading lamp off the desk in the back room and carried it through and set it on the floor on her side of the bed with the shade turned so that the light came up onto her at the angle we use — low, oblique, from below the plane of the face, because light from above fills the ground and light from below throws the lines and any reader who tells you otherwise is reading portraits and not people. I put a folded towel under the lamp so the base would not scrape.
I sat on the floor with my back against the wardrobe.
Then I did not do anything for perhaps twenty minutes, and I have no account of that twenty minutes. I was not deciding. The deciding had happened in the stationer's.
Then I read my wife.
The scalp line first, because you always start at the top of the page, because that is the discipline and the discipline is the only thing that keeps a reader from finding what he came to find.

It was intact. Temple to temple, full and level, no retreat. In a woman of forty-four that is a strong first line and it always had been. But the ground under the right temple had gone down, and a line does not have to move to change: if the surface beneath it drops, the line curves in space even though every hair is where it was. It had begun to bow. Not much. Less than the width of a fingernail.
A straight stroke that has taken a shallow curve at one end is a different letter than a straight stroke.
I did not write that down yet. I went to the brows.

The right brow had dropped — I have already told you it had dropped, I knew that in the doctor's office in the first four minutes — but under the lamp, from below, at two in the morning, what I saw was not a drop. It was a tilt. The inner end had stayed where it was, anchored beside the sword-cut. The outer end had gone down and, because the temple had hollowed, slightly back. So the brow was no longer a horizontal stroke with a rise in it. It was an oblique, running down and away from the line of settling.
An oblique running down and away from the centre.
I sat on the floor of my bedroom and my ears went hot, the way they do.

Because I knew what that was. Any child in this lineage knows what that is. It is the descender. It is the tail that hangs below the ruled line, the stroke that a scribe pulls down and out at the end of a word to say this is finished, this closes here — and there are seven letters in Persian that carry one and the doctrine reads all seven of them under the same head: completion.
Her right brow had stopped being a line and become an ending.

I read for another hour and forty minutes. Lashes, four sets, the two on the right now sitting at a changed angle over an eye that did not fully close and therefore showed more of itself, which alters the ground and therefore alters the contrast and therefore alters everything. The tuft, which she did not have. The nostrils, which she did not have. Seven lines and four of them altered and one of them altered into something that had a name.
And at four in the morning I sat there with my hands over my mouth, because the reading I had just taken off my wife's sleeping face was better than any reading I had ever taken off her.
I do not mean more pleasant. Do not misunderstand me, I am not going to tell you her disease was writing her a love letter.

I mean better as a text. Denser. More determined. The old reading — the one I had had of her since I was twenty-four years old, the one I had taken in a room with two families in it and a plate of sweets on the table — was clear, and it was fine, and it was, I understood on that floor, bland. Seven strong lines all agreeing with each other, all level, all saying more or less the same thing in the same tone. A fair copy of an unremarkable document. A face like good handwriting on a form.

And now four of the seven had gone off in different directions and started arguing, and one of them had a tail on it, and the whole page had acquired the quality that I had spent twenty-six years telling apprentices was the mark of an important text and which I could not, that night, remember ever having found in a living person.
It had become difficult.

She turned over at twenty past four and I picked the lamp up off the floor with both hands so that it would not scrape and carried it back to the desk in the dark, and I did not sleep, and at seven she came into the kitchen taping her eye shut with one hand and said, "You look terrible," and I said the fog had kept me up, which is not even a lie a person can tell, and she took it and went to put the kettle on.
The notebook was A5, hard cover, black, ninety pages.
I want to describe what I actually did with it because I have heard the versions that circulate now and they are all more dramatic than the truth and the truth is worse.

I did not write it up like scripture. I did not use the formulas. There is a formula — there is a whole liturgical shape to a written reading, the position and the date and the light and the reader's name and then the fourteen or the seven each on their own line with their value and their letter and then the sentence at the bottom, and I have written perhaps four hundred of them in my life for the lineage's archive, in a hand I inherited from Ostad Rafi'i, who inherited it from his mother.
I wrote it up like a man writing about his wife.
4th month, 21st. 02:10–04:20. Lamp low from left, floor. She slept the whole time.
Scalp: intact, bowing at right temple. Perhaps 2mm of drop under it since the photograph at Nowruz. The line has not moved. The ground has moved.
Right brow: descender. It is a descender. I have looked at it for an hour and I cannot make it anything else.

And then, four lines further down, in the same hand, on the same page, and this is the sentence that eleven months later a woman of seventy-one read aloud, in a flat voice, in my own back room, to everyone I have:
I have never had this much from her.
That is what I wrote. Six words. I have never had this much from her.

Not she has never given me this much. Not the text has never offered this much. I have never had this much from her — a man's sentence, an appetite's sentence, and the woman it is about was asleep eight feet away with a piece of clear tape holding her eye shut.
I went back nine more times over the next six weeks.

It stopped being a Thursday thing. It became whatever night the light was right and she was under by eleven, and I got better at it, which is the part I would most like to leave out. I learned to fold a second towel under the lamp base. I learned that if I ran the tap in the bathroom first she would surface and turn and go deeper and then I had two hours instead of one. I learned to take the lamp back before I wrote anything, so that if she woke there was nothing in the room to explain.

I hid the notebook inside the dust jacket of the second volume of my father's commentary, on the high shelf, behind the door, which is exactly where a man in this city hides money and exactly where his wife looks for it.
And every one of those nine readings was better than the one before.

That is the part I need you to sit with, because everyone who hears this story wants there to have been a moment where I saw what I was doing and chose it anyway, a moment of clean transgression with a door in it.
There was no door. There was a page that got more interesting every week.

If the readings had been bad — if the illness had smeared her, blurred the lines, thickened the ground, made her hard to read the way age makes people hard to read — I would have stopped in the second week and grieved like anybody else, and this would be a short book about a man whose wife got sick.
Instead I was being handed, night after night, in my own bedroom, off the face of the person I loved most in the world, the finest text I had ever read.

And I did not tell her. And I did not tell the lineage. And on the ninth night, in the sixth week, with the lamp on the floor and the towel folded under it, I found that the outer third of her right brow was no longer there at all, and I put my hand out and did not quite touch her face, and I wrote in the notebook: six.
Not she has lost her eyebrow.
Six.
PART SIX — THE UPPER LEFT LASHES
Six.

There is no word in our books for six. There are words for the seven and words for the fourteen and words for the twenty-eight and words for the thirty-two, and there is a great deal of writing about what it means that these numbers are what they are, and about the seven verses of the Fatiha, and the seven cavities of the head — two eye sockets, two nostrils, two earholes, the mouth — and about the thirty-two teeth, which Fazlallah offered as the body's own signature on the alphabet.
There is nothing about six.

Six is not a diminished seven in our system. It is not seven-minus-one. Our numbers do not work by subtraction, they work by completion, and a set that is not complete is not a smaller set. It is a different kind of object entirely, and there is no name for it, and the reason there is no name for it is that until the winter I am describing, no one in six hundred years had needed one.

Everybody has seven. That is the whole point of the maternal lines. That is why they are the maternal lines. Every child born on the earth arrives with the scalp line and two brows and four sets of lashes, and this universality is not incidental to the doctrine, it is the doctrine — it is the proof that the alphabet is issued to all and withheld from none, that God does not write only on the beautiful or the rich or the male, that the poorest infant in the poorest house in this province is a complete document from the moment it opens its eyes.
Seven is the floor. Nobody has ever been under the floor.
My wife was under the floor.
I cried for the first time that night, on the floor of our bedroom, with my hand over my mouth so hard that I bruised my lip.
And here is my problem, and it is the problem I have not solved in the time since and will not solve in this book:
I do not know what I was crying about.

There is the obvious answer. My wife, forty-four years old, was being taken apart in front of me over months, without pain, without pause, and there was nothing at the end of it that anyone had been able to describe to me as a stopping place, and I loved her, and I had loved her since I was twenty-four, and a man is entitled to sit on the floor and cry about that.

And there is the other answer, which arrived at the same time and in the same body, and which I could not separate from the first one that night and cannot separate now: that I was holding the only text in the recorded history of my people that had gone under seven, and that it was the greatest thing I would ever read, and that it was still going, and that no reader in six hundred years had been given what I had been given.
Both of those were true at four in the morning.

I have talked to two people about this. One of them, who is dead now, told me that grief is not clean in anyone and that I was making a virtue of my own bookkeeping. The other one said nothing for a long time and then said, "Which one made you write it down?"
I wrote it down.
THE THIRD RECITATION
Delivered on the eighth night, at the house of Tuba Khanum.
Fifteen adults, the room too small for it, people standing at the back. Word had begun to move.
After the head came off at Alinja, the doctrine did not die. It went sideways, which is what doctrines do.

Some of his followers decided he would come back. That is the ordinary thing, and it is a little sad, and it is not our line. Others decided something stranger and much more dangerous, which is our line, and which explains this room and everyone in it, and which I want you to hear properly because people repeat it as though it were a joke about heretics.
They decided they were already in Paradise.

The reasoning is airtight if you accept the first step. If Fazlallah was the manifestation of the glory, and if to have seen him was to have had the vision of God that the rest of the faithful are promised only after death — then those who saw him have already received the reward. They are in the garden now, standing here, in these clothes.
And there are no duties in Paradise.

So: no prayer. No fast. No ritual washing. Nothing forbidden, nothing required, nothing unclean. One of our own texts puts it flatly — Paradise is knowledge and hellfire is ignorance, and a man who knows the thirty-two of his own being holds all things as permitted.
Some of them went further than that and said that a man who has the knowledge is entitled to take whatever comes within his reach, and to go and get what does not.

I am not going to soften this. This is in our books. This is what a portion of our people believed in Baghdad and Shirvan and Gilan [gee-LAAN] and Khorasan, and it is one of the several reasons the world came for us with fire.
But I want the young ones in this room to understand what it left us with, because you are living inside the consequence of it and you do not know that you are.
We have no machinery for forbidding.

Look around this room. Count us. Three families. We have a reader, we have an elder, we have an archive in four houses and a rite in the month he died. We have no clergy. We have no court. We have never, in six centuries, tried anyone for anything, because the men who carried this doctrine out of the fifteenth century carried it out on the specific understanding that prohibition is a thing that belongs to the world outside the garden.
Every other faith on this earth, when one of its own does something monstrous, has a lever to pull.
We have a lever for one thing only, and it is not forbidding, and you will hear what it is on the last night.
Now: Aleppo.

His name was Nesimi [neh-see-MEE], and he was the best poet any of us have ever produced, and he met Fazlallah exactly once, shortly before the end. Once. That was enough to ruin a man for the rest of his life and Nesimi spent the rest of his walking through Anatolia putting the doctrine into Turkish verse so good that people who despised the doctrine copied out the poems anyway.
And into the poems he put a sentence that was not ours. He took it from Hallaj [hal-LAAJ], the great martyr of the Sufis, executed in Baghdad four hundred years before him for saying it in public.
Ana'l-Haqq [a-nal-HAQQ]. I am the Truth. Which is to say: I am God.

Our scholars have argued for centuries about whether they killed him for the letters or for that sentence. I think it was the sentence. I think the letters were an eccentricity and the sentence was a capital crime, and I think it hardly matters, because the two of them are the same claim wearing different clothes: if the divine writing is on your face, then the thing walking around inside the writing is going to say something like ana'l-Haqq eventually, and the world is going to answer.
They flayed him alive.
In Aleppo, in the first decade of the fifteenth century — the year is disputed among the historians and I have never understood why anyone thought the year was the interesting part.
I said to you on the sixth night that our founder's punishment took his face off his body. Hear what this one is.
This one takes the face off the face.

A flaying does not remove a man. It removes his surface. It removes the exact substance — skin, and what grows out of skin — on which every one of the fourteen lines is written. It leaves the man; for a while, it leaves the man very much there. And it takes the page.

There is a story that he went on reciting while it was done. I do not know whether it is true. I do not think it is true. I have sat with the dying for twenty-six years and I know what a body will and will not do.
But I understand exactly why we tell it, and so do you.
Because the whole of our doctrine is the claim that the writing is not the surface.

That the letters are not ink. That the face is not a picture of the scripture but the scripture itself, and therefore inexhaustible, and therefore not the kind of thing that can be taken off a man with a knife and held up.
And the only way to make that claim in front of a man being skinned in a public square in Aleppo is to say that he kept talking.
Here the recitation ends. Tonight the tea was late, because there were not enough glasses in the house, and Golnaz
Ehsani went next door for more.
PART SEVEN — THE LOWER LEFT LASHES
Sanam found the notebook. Not Tuba Khanum.

I have let people believe otherwise for a long time, because Tuba Khanum let them, and because the version in which the elder discovers the reader's secret is a tidier story than the one in which a sick woman goes looking for money behind her husband's father's commentaries.
She was looking for money. We had begun to need it. The scans are not free and the drops are not free and I had not read a paid funeral in five weeks because I had stopped answering the phone.
She took it down and read nine entries and put it back and said nothing for four days.

Four days. She poured tea. She asked me about Golnaz's progress. She watched a programme about the fisheries. On the fourth night she sat down across from me at the kitchen table with the notebook in front of her and her hands flat on either side of it, and the light was bad, and I remember that the right side of her face was the side toward the window, so that the sword-cut had a shadow lying in it, and I remember noticing that, and I remember hating myself in a way I had not managed at any point in the previous four months.
"Read it to me," she said.
"Sanam—"
"You have read me nine times. Read it to me."
So I read my wife the transcript of her own face.

It took forty minutes. She stopped me twice. The first time was at the line has not moved, the ground has moved, and she said, "Say that again," and I said it again, and she nodded once and told me to go on. The second time was at I have never had this much from her, and she did not say anything at all, and I stopped by myself, and then after a while I kept going because she was waiting.
At the end she said: "Is it good?"
"What?"
"The reading. Not — is it kind. Is it good. As a piece of work. Would your teacher have said it was good."
I said: "It is the best thing I have ever done."
And my wife put her head back and laughed with half her mouth, and it was a real laugh, and it was the most frightening sound I have ever heard in that house.
"Twenty-four years," she said. "Twenty-four years of being a cereal box. And all I had to do was this."

Then she said the thing that I did not understand for another eleven months, and that I have decided to put down here exactly where it happened rather than where it becomes clear, because you should have the same chance I had and did not take.
She said: "Do you want to know what frightens me?"
"Yes."

"Not the illness." She turned the notebook around with one finger, so it faced me. "That it took this. That there was a version of my face that got your attention and I did not have it. That somebody could have given me this, at the start, and you would have looked at me like that for twenty-four years."
I said something. I said something reasonable and warm and wrong, about how she had always been legible to me, about how a fair copy is not a lesser copy.
She let me finish. She was always very good about letting me finish.
Then she said, "Take it to Tuba Khanum."
"No."
"Mansur. You are going to take it to her eventually, and you will do it in a way that makes you look better than you look tonight. Take it now. Tonight, while I have said yes."
"You are saying yes?"
"I am saying," said Sanam, "that if this is happening to me, I would like to have been the one who let it happen."
That is exactly what she said. I have never written it down until now.
She thought she was choosing. I let her think it, because it was easier for both of us, and because I wanted to go, and because a man who wants to go will accept any permission he is handed.
They ratified it on a Friday afternoon in the front room of Tuba Khanum's house, with the three families in it and nowhere left to sit.
I want to describe how ordinary it was.

There was no vote. We do not have votes. There was no formula; nobody knew a formula for this because there had never been an occasion for one. Tuba Khanum sat in the good chair with the notebook on her knee and read the nine entries aloud in a flat voice, the way she reads everything, and when she got to I have never had this much from her she did not pause and did not look up, and I have thought about that for a long time and I believe she was protecting me, and I believe she should not have.
Then she closed it and put her hand on the cover and said: "Well. It is a reading."
That was the whole thing. Four words.

An old woman in a chair in a provincial city saying well, it is a reading, and a room full of people understanding immediately and completely what had just been decided, and one man standing by the door with his coat still on, feeling something come up through the floor of his chest that he did not have a name for and that he would like to record here was not entirely horror.
Because I want to be very clear about what happened in that room, and about why it happened, and about how it could not have happened any other way.
They did not approve of me. Several of them did not, and two of them have not spoken to me since.
They ratified — which is a different act, and a colder one. Ratification is what you do when a thing has occurred and your system contains no instrument for un-occurring it.
Think about what they would have needed, to stop it.

They would have needed a rule that says a reader may not read a particular face. There is no such rule; the entire doctrine is that any face may be read by anyone with the discipline, because that universality is the thing that makes it revelation instead of privilege.

They would have needed a rule that says a text in motion is not scripture. There is no such rule, and worse, everything in our books runs the other way — the Javdan-nama is emphatic that the writing is living, that creation is continuous, that God did not write once and stop.
They would have needed a doctrine of the forbidden.
And we sold that, six hundred years ago, in Shirvan and Gilan and Baghdad, for the extraordinary and terrible freedom of believing ourselves already in the garden.

Tuba Khanum said, well, it is a reading, because within our doctrine that is a true and complete sentence and there is nothing further available to say. It was a reading. It had been taken by a qualified reader, in proper light, from a face that possessed lines. Whether the face belonged to his sleeping wife, whether he had wanted her to have it, whether the whole thing was the most sordid act any of us had ever committed — none of that is a category in our books. Our books contain the number of the lines and the values of the letters and the discipline of the light.
A doctrine that will not forbid anything cannot protect anyone.
That is the sentence. That is the thing I have to say in this book and I would rather say it here, at the halfway point, plainly, than dress it up later.

We spent six centuries congratulating ourselves that we had no clergy and no court and no inquisitor. We told each other that this was our purity: that we were the only people who had ever taken the writing seriously enough to refuse to police it. Every one of the recitations you have heard so far is, in part, a story about how the people with courts and inquisitors came and burned us, and we recite them with the particular satisfaction of the persecuted, who always believe that being killed for a thing proves the thing.
It proves nothing at all.
And on that Friday, a roomful of people who had no lever to pull looked at a man who had done something to his wife in the dark, and reached for the only instrument our doctrine has ever contained.
They read it.
The visits began nine days later.
PART EIGHT — THE RIGHT CHEEK
the first paternal line, from Adam
Five.
The upper right lashes went over about three weeks, and they did not fall out. I want to be accurate because the difference matters to a reader and it mattered to me.

Hair that falls out leaves a bare line. The line is gone but the place of the line is still there, a strip of skin where something used to be, and a reader can work with that; we have a whole procedure for the burned and the bald and the ones who have had the drugs, and the short version of the procedure is that an erased line still tells you where it was erased from.

Hers did not fall out. The ground under them dropped, and the lid rolled slightly outward as it dropped, and the lashes went with it — turned, until they were no longer a stroke lying across the eye but a fringe pointing away from me. Still present. Still every hair. Not readable, from any angle, in any light, because a line that has turned edge-on to the reader is not a line, it is a row of points.
I spent four nights trying to get an angle on them and on the fifth I wrote five and closed the book.
The visits had been going eleven weeks by then.
Nine days after they ratified it, the first one came. After that I stopped being able to say when any of them came, because they arrived the way weather arrives.

They took their shoes off in the hall. They sat in the back room under the north window, with my wife's face at the right height and the right distance, for two hours at a stretch, and made their notes, and thanked her on the way out, and thanked me, and I have never in my life been thanked in that particular way.

By the fourth week there was a rota — a list, with days on it, saying who came when. I did not make it. Tuba Khanum says she did not make it, and I believe her, and that is the most disturbing sentence in this chapter. It simply came into existence, the way a path appears across a field, because a great many people all wanted the same thing at the same rate and were too polite to jostle.
By the eighth week we had a chair in the back room that was not one of our chairs, brought by somebody, left behind, and then used, and then permanent.

They took their shoes off. They brought food. They were, without exception, kind to her, and several of them were kinder to her than I was in that period, and I know that because I watched them do it.
And every one of them, for two hours at a stretch, sat eight inches from my wife's face and did not see her.

That is not a figure of speech and I am not accusing them of coldness. It is a technical fact about the discipline. You cannot read a face and see a person at the same time. The whole training is a training in not seeing the person — in refusing the mouth's expression, refusing the eyes, refusing the small movements that a face makes to tell you how it feels about you, because all of that is weather and you are there for the geology. I taught this. I have said in that same room, to that same third family, the sentence: if you can still tell whether she likes you, you are not reading yet.
They came into my house and did to my wife, correctly and with great care, a thing whose first requirement is that she not be a person.
And she made them tea.
I asked her, once, in the tenth week, why she allowed it.
She was drying her hands. She took a long time about it.

"Because you have all decided that I am the most important thing that has happened to this family in six hundred years," she said, "and there is no version of me saying stop that does not end with you hating me. Not out loud. You would all be extremely gracious about it."
"That is not true."
"Mansur." She hung the cloth on the rail. "How many nights since Nowruz have you slept?"
I did not answer.
"You would forgive me," she said. "You would forgive me the way a man forgives a fire."
THE FOURTH RECITATION

Delivered on the tenth night. It had been moved out to the courtyard, under plastic sheeting, with the heaters, because the house would not hold the number who came. This had not been necessary in living memory.
Thirty-seven years after Alinja, in Isfahan, a man we know almost nothing about led the last rising.

They called him Haji Sorkh [haa-JEE SORKH] — the red pilgrim — and he was not from Isfahan [es-fa-HAAN]; he arrived from somewhere else and within a short time he had enough of the city's Hurufis behind him to attack the governor's household and kill two of the governor's sons.

It failed. They always failed. Read our history in one sitting and what you notice is not the persecution, it is the incompetence — a doctrine that produced the finest poets in three languages could not organise a stable rebellion in a hundred years, and I have come to think the two facts are the same fact. A people who believe that the divine is already complete on every face have no reason to go anywhere or build anything. What would you build? The building would be less than the doorman's forehead.
They took Haji Sorkh and they skinned him alive.
Second time.

I said at Aleppo that the punishment takes the face off the face. Here it is again, thirty years later, a different city, a different court, a different crime — a rebellion this time, an ordinary political crime with ordinary political rage behind it — and they reach for the same knife.
Nobody was making a point.

That is what I want the young ones to understand and it is the hardest thing in this recitation to say without sounding as though I am claiming a pattern. There is no conspiracy in it. Flaying was a real punishment in the fifteenth century and it was used on people who had never heard of the letters. If I told you the burnings and the beheadings of that century you would find our people scattered thinly among thousands of others, punished in all the ordinary ways for all the ordinary reasons.
But we do not recite the century. We recite ourselves.

And when a people recites only itself, over six hundred years, on ten nights a year, in courtyards, to children — a shape emerges out of the coincidences, and the shape is true in the only way that matters, which is that it is now what we are made of.
Ours is this. Every time the world has come for us, it has come for the surface.
The head off the body. The skin off the man. The skin off the man again.

And in ten nights' time you will hear how it ended, and you will hear that the last time, they did not take anyone's face at all. They took the room. They took five hundred of them at once and there was nothing left to read, and one of the five hundred was the woman who had copied out the book with her own hand, which is the only reason any of us can say any of this to you tonight.
I have been asked, by people who are not of us, whether we are frightened.
Whether living inside a story like this — a story whose every chapter ends with a face being removed — does something to a person over a lifetime.
The honest answer is no, and the honest answer is a confession.

We are not frightened, because it is finished. Nobody is coming. There has not been a fatwa against this doctrine in four hundred years for the excellent reason that nobody outside these three families believes it exists. We are not persecuted. We are not hidden. We are a small number of people in a provincial city who file our taxes and send our children to school and read faces, and the last person to die for this died in a century that had no rifles in it.
We recite the flayings the way a family recites a bankruptcy two generations back. With feeling. With a certain pride. From complete safety.
And that is why, when something finally did come for one of our faces — quietly, from inside, over months, in a bedroom — nobody in this courtyard recognised it.
We had six hundred years of practice at the wrong danger.
Here the recitation ends. The heaters were turned down. It rained on the plastic for the whole of the tea.
PART NINE — THE LEFT CHEEK
By midsummer the house was not a house.

I do not mean that in the way people mean it. The rooms were the same. Nobody had moved anything except the chair. What had changed was that every object in it had acquired a second function, the way objects do in a shop, so that the north window was no longer a window but the light, and the kitchen table was no longer where we ate but where the transcripts were collated on Fridays, and the corridor was where you waited.
There was a folder on the shelf by the door with the rota in it.
There was a plastic box for the shoes.

And there was a system for the photographs, which had begun with one camera on a kitchen chair and had become, by midsummer, a tripod and a strip of white tape on the floor to stand it on. The whole worth of a run of photographs is that nothing moves between them except the face. Shift the camera half an inch and you cannot tell afterwards whether the face changed or the room did.

They photographed her every eleven days. It had to be eleven; I do not remember who decided eleven or why, and by the time I thought to ask, eleven had been the interval for months and asking would have seemed like an attack.

She sat on a stool. She looked at a mark on the wall. She held still for the count of five, twice, and then she got up and went to put the kettle on, and behind her the sequence went into the folder and the folder went into the archive and the archive is in four houses in this province and will outlast every person named in this book.
I want to put down here what I understood at the time, because it was not nothing, and because I have been given more credit for blindness than I deserve.

I understood that my wife had become an object of study. I understood that this had happened because of a notebook I hid behind my father's commentaries. I understood that the kindness of the visitors — and it was real kindness, they were not monsters, they brought food and asked after her sister and took their shoes off — was the specific kindness that people extend to something valuable, and that the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside, and completely impossible to tell apart from where she was sitting.
What I did not understand was that there was a version of this that was worse than exploitation.

Exploitation I could have got my hands around. Exploitation has somebody behind it. If they had been using my wife, I could have stood up in that courtyard and said so, and there would have been a fight, and fights end.
Nobody was using her.

Every single one of them believed — correctly, according to everything our doctrine has ever said — that they were doing the highest thing anyone of our tradition can do: sitting with a revelation while it is being given. They were not taking from her. They were witnessing. And the reason they came on Tuesdays and Thursdays with food and left their shoes in a plastic box was that they thought they were the luckiest people alive.
You cannot fight that. You cannot even name it without sounding like a man who wants his wife to himself.
She stopped me in the corridor on a Thursday in the ninth month, after the last of them had gone, with the light off, and said:
"I want to tell you what is actually happening."
I said all right.
"Not to my face. To me."

We sat in the kitchen. She did not put the light on. I have thought a great deal about the fact that she did not put the light on, and I have concluded that it was not shame, it was that she had spent nine months being lit correctly and she wanted one conversation in the dark.
"You have all written down," she said, "what my face says. Yes?"
"Yes."
"Read me the last one."
"Sanam—"
"From memory. You know it from memory."

I did know it from memory. I said: "The scalp line has taken a bow at the right temple and no longer runs true. The right brow is a descender. The upper right lashes have turned edge-on and cannot be read. The lower right are shortening. What remains legible is four lines and a fragment, and the fragment is arguing with the four."
"Arguing," she said.
"That is the word we use when—"

"I know the word you use. I have been in this house for twenty-four years." She put both hands flat on the table. "Now listen to me, because this is the part that nobody has written down and nobody is going to.

"I cannot close my right eye. I tape it shut to sleep and in the morning the tape takes skin off and I have got used to that. I cannot feel the right side of my top lip and I have not been able to since the spring, so when I drink I have to watch myself in the window of the microwave to know whether I am spilling. Food goes into the pocket on that side and stays there and I have to hook it out with a finger, and I do that in the bathroom with the door locked, four or five times a day, and I have never once done it in front of you.

"Chewing is on one side. My jaw aches all the time on the good side from doing all of it. I bite the inside of my cheek because I cannot feel where it is, so there is a place in there that never gets a chance to heal and it has been there since Ramadan.
"I have stopped going to my sister's because her children stare, and they are not being cruel, they are four and six.

"And two weeks ago in the bazaar a woman I have known since school looked straight at me and did not know me. She looked at me and sorted me — you know how it goes, that fast little movement, into the pile of people you do not know — and she smiled the way you smile at a stranger who is standing too close, and she moved on.
"That is what is happening. That is the whole event, from the inside. It is spilling water and hooking food out of a pocket and a woman not knowing me in the bazaar."
She stopped. Then she said:
"Not one word of that is in the archive."

I said — and I would give a great deal to be able to write down something else here — I said that it was in the archive, that the fourth reading records an eyelid that will not shut and the seventh notes a top lip gone slack, that it was all there.
She sat in the dark and let me say it.
Then she said: "You have recorded that my lip does not work. You have not recorded that I hide in the bathroom."
"That is not—" I stopped.
"Say it."
"That is not what the discipline is for."
"No," she said. "It is not. Thank you."
She got up and filled the kettle at the tap by feel, in the dark, and stood with her back to me.

"I am not asking you to stop. I have thought about it for weeks and I am not asking that; you would stop and it would be worse, you would sit in this house with all that not-doing in you and I would have to watch it. I am asking for one thing.
"When I die, and you read me — and it will be you, do not let them give it to anyone else, I have told Tuba Khanum and she has agreed — when you read me, at the funeral, in front of everyone.
"Say one thing that is not on my face."
I said: "What thing?"
"You have twenty-four years," said my wife. "Find one."
PART TEN — THE RIGHT MOUSTACHE
The lower right lashes went in the eleventh month and the count came to four, and the lineage split.

I had not expected that. I had expected grief, or a kind of solemnity, or at worst the sour undertone that had been in two of the families since the ratification. What I got was six weeks of the most vicious scholarly argument I have witnessed in my life, conducted entirely in polite voices, in the courtyard and on the telephone and in a series of letters written by people who lived four streets apart.
The question was the scalp line.

By then the ground under her right temple had gone far enough that the hairline on that side did not merely bow — it broke. There was a section, perhaps two fingers wide, where the hair had gone down with the ground beneath it, so that the line ran from the left temple, across the crown, and then stopped, and then resumed for a short distance at the right temple and ended.
A line with a gap in it.
And the whole lineage discovered, in a single week, that we had no ruling on a broken line.
I will give you both sides, because I have to, because I argued one of them and I no longer know if I believed it.

The first position. A line is a line by virtue of being one continuous stroke.
