Break it and you do not have a line with a defect; you have two short lines, neither of which is any of the seven, because the seven are named and enumerated and there is no eighth. Therefore the scalp line is gone. Therefore the count is three.

The second position. The seven are not seven strokes. They are seven places — seven regions of the face at which the divine writing is issued. Interruption within a place is a feature of the writing, not a deletion of it; every old book in the world has damage in it and nobody says a torn page has stopped being scripture. Therefore the scalp line is present, and altered, and the count is four.
They argued that for six weeks.

A doctrine six hundred years old, three surviving families, and every scholar the tradition had left in the world — and all of it was thrown at the question of whether a woman's hairline still counted.
Nobody asked her.
I want that on the page by itself.
Nobody asked her.
It settled at four, in the end, and it settled the way these things always settle, which is that Tuba Khanum stopped talking about it and everyone noticed that she had stopped.
I wrote four in the notebook on a Tuesday in the twelfth month.
And I sat there with the pen and I did not put it down for a long time, because of what four is.
Four is not one of our numbers either. Seven, fourteen, twenty-eight, thirty-two — those are our numbers, those are the ones the books are about. There is no chapter on four.
But there is a four.

There are four letters in the Persian alphabet that Arabic does not have. Pe [PEH]. Che [CHEH]. Zhe [ZHEH]. Gaf [GAAF]. They are the sounds in pedar, father; in chesm, eye; in the middle of muzhde, good news; in gol, flower — four sounds a Persian mouth makes and an Arab mouth does not.

Any scholar in the world will tell you where they came from. Scribes made them. They took Arabic letters that already existed and added dots to them, centuries after the revelation had closed, because they needed to write their own language down. Four letters that arrived late, by human hand, in a workshop.

And Fazlallah, in the book that this entire lineage has organised itself around for six hundred years, insisted that those four were pre-eternal. That they were among the names taught to Adam before time. That the men who improvised them were not inventing but remembering, and that there is no test anywhere in creation that can tell a letter God wrote from a letter a man added in good faith.
Four.
I looked at that number on the page in my own handwriting for I do not know how long, and I did not write anything under it, and I closed the book.

I want to be honest about what that was. It was not a revelation. I did not sit up. It was the sensation you get when two things in a room turn out to be the same colour and you cannot stop seeing it, and there is no meaning in it, and you know there is no meaning in it, and you look at it anyway.
Two months later a nineteen-year-old girl told me where she got her nose, and the colour stopped being a coincidence.
THE FIFTH RECITATION

Delivered on the twelfth night, in the courtyard, without the sheeting, because it was dry. Sanam Sarmadi attended, and sat, and was moved three separate times into the seat with the best light on her, by three different people, none of whom had planned it. She remarked on this afterwards to me and to nobody else.
Tabriz [tab-REEZ]. Forty-seven years after Alinja.
This is the last one. After tonight there are no more killings to recite, and the reason is not that they stopped disliking us. It is that after Tabriz there was nobody left in Persia to kill.

The community there was large and it was confident and it had, for the first and only time in our history, something like a patron: the ruler of the city wrote poetry, and in his poetry — you can still read it — he praised Fazlallah by name, and he wrote that the seven verses of the opening chapter of the Qur'an are reflected in the face of the beloved.
Hold on to that line. I am going to come back to it and it is going to cost you something.

The community was led, in part, by a woman. She was Fazlallah's own daughter. Her name was Kalimat-Allah al-'Ulya [ka-lee-MAT ol-LAAH al-OOL-yaa] — the Word of God, the Exalted — which tells you everything about the family she was born into, and she had been widowed by a butcher who died in a fit of ecstasy in the Naubar [now-BAR] quarter of that city, and she had spent her life doing the thing that keeps doctrines alive, which is not preaching.
Copying.

The scholars of Tabriz demanded the ruler destroy us. He did not want to. He temporised for years. And then a dervish came to the leading scholar of the city and said that the Prophet had appeared to him in a dream and instructed that the Hurufis be annihilated.
A dream.

Our founder was a dream-interpreter before he was anything else. People brought him their dreams the way you bring a doctor a cough. That is how he made his living in his twenties, in the city where you are sitting.
And it was a dream that killed us.
The scholar issued the ruling. The ruler stood out of the way. And they burned around five hundred people in Tabriz, and one of them was the daughter, and there is no grave.
Now. Two things, and then we will have the tea.

The first. I told you at Aleppo and at Isfahan that when the world comes for us it comes for the surface. That is the shape of our story. Here it does not hold. Here they did not take faces. They took a room and everything in it, and there was no page left, no skin, nothing to hold up in a square.

That is worse and you know it is worse, and I have never met a person of this lineage who could say exactly why. I think it is this: a flaying leaves a text. There is a thing on the ground that was the writing. What happened in Tabriz left no object at all. It is the only event in six hundred years of our history that produced nothing to read.
The second, and this is why we recite this one last.

Everything we possess — every book in the four houses, every commentary, the summary in Persian, the pages in the old dialect that none of us can properly read, every last thing that lets me stand in a courtyard and tell you what a hairline means — exists because that woman sat down and copied out her father's book by hand.

She made copies. The copies went out. The copies went west, into Anatolia, into the Balkans, into the lodges of dervishes who were not us and did not care what we believed and kept our books for five hundred years anyway, on shelves, in Albania, for reasons nobody has satisfactorily explained.
She burned. Her copies did not.
That is the doctrine's one hard-won piece of practical wisdom and I want the young ones to have it plainly:
We do not survive in bodies. We survive in copies.

Here the recitation ends. This is the last of the killings. On the fourteenth night we recite the crossing, and the six hundred years of nothing, and then we recite ourselves, and then the month is over.
PART ELEVEN — THE LEFT MOUSTACHE
Golnaz told me in the back room, on a Tuesday, with the light going, and she did it in the flat voice people use when they have rehearsed a thing in the car.
"I need to say something and I need you to not talk until I finish."
"All right."
"When I was seventeen I had my nose done."
I did not say anything, because she had asked me not to, and because there was nothing in me that wanted to.

"And my brows. Not plucked — everyone does plucked. Threaded and then the ends taken up. And the hairline, a little, at the temples, because I have my father's temples." She had her hands under her thighs, palms down, sitting on them, which is what she did when she was frightened, and which I had noticed in her first week and had never mentioned to her. "I begged my mother for a year. She said no for a year. Then she said yes and paid for it and told my father it was for my sinuses."
"Golnaz—"
"You said you would not talk."
"You have finished."

"I have not finished." She took her hands out from under her legs and put them on the table. "I have been sitting in this room for fourteen months learning that my face is the writing of God. And I have known the whole time that a woman in a room off the ring road took a knife to it when I was seventeen because I would not stop crying about it."

The light went while she was saying that. It goes fast here in the autumn; there is a particular ten minutes when the north window stops being useful and I have spent my life arranging myself around those ten minutes, and I did not get up to turn the lamp on, because getting up would have been a way of leaving.
We sat in the dark.
"Say something," she said.
"I do not have anything."
"You have twenty-six years."
"I have twenty-six years of a doctrine that does not have a sentence for you." I heard my own voice do something I did not like. "Do you want the school answer or do you want what I actually think?"
"The school answer first."
So I gave her the school answer, and I will give it to you, because it is coherent and it is old and until that autumn I believed it.
To alter a face is not vandalism. It is forgery.

That is the whole of it, and everything else is commentary. We do not say that a surgeon has damaged the writing, because damage is a category we are comfortable with — every face is damaged, by weather and work and years, and a damaged manuscript is still the manuscript. Scars are legible. Burns are legible. A man who has been kicked by a horse at nine years old has a face that a good reader can read around, and the reading will include the horse, because the horse happened to him and God did not stop writing when the horse arrived.
Forgery is different in kind. Forgery is when a hand that is not the author's makes marks that are impossible to tell apart from the author's, with intent that they be read as the author's.

The forged face does not say nothing. That is what people always assume and it is exactly wrong. The forged face says something perfectly clear, in good letters, in a confident hand — and what it says did not come from God, and it will be read as though it did, by a reader who has no way of knowing, in front of a family who will believe him.
That is why it is the great crime in our books and the only thing approaching one. Not because it insults the writing. Because it corrupts the reading.

And I told her — and this is the part I would take back — that it was not her sin. That she was seventeen. That the sin belongs to the hand that holds the blade and not to the face that was on the table.
She listened to all of it in the dark.
Then she said: "And what do you actually think?"
"I think it does not matter whose sin it is," I said. "I think I have read you eleven times and written six of them into the archive and I do not know which parts of you I was reading."
"Yes," said Golnaz. "That is what I think too."
Then, after a while, in a different voice, the voice of a girl and not of a student:
"Everyone has had it done."
"Not everyone."

"Ostad. Everyone." She said it patiently, the way you correct someone about a thing they have decided not to look at. "In my year at school, out of thirty-one girls, I know of nineteen. Two hundred thousand a year in this country. There are streets in Tehran where you cannot buy a sandwich but you can get a nose. My cousin had hers done twice because the first one settled wrong."
"That is Tehran."
"It is Gorgan. It is this street." She leaned forward. "Ostad, when you read a face in this city, and the face is under fifty, and it is a woman — what odds are you giving yourself?"
I did not answer her.
"You have never asked," she said. "Not once, in any reading, in your whole life, have you asked a woman whether her face is hers."
"It would be an obscene question."

"It would be the first question you would have to ask to do the job properly," said Golnaz Ehsani, nineteen years old, sitting in my dead teacher's chair in the dark, "and you have not asked it because you already knew what the answer was going to be, and you would rather have the readings."

The place is called the Darmangah-e Nur [dar-maan-GAAH-eh NOOR]. The Light Clinic. It is on the ring road between a tyre place and a shuttered bank, and it has been there since before I was married, and I had driven past it perhaps four thousand times.
That is not a figure of speech. I did the arithmetic afterwards, sitting in the car. Twice a week for thirty years to get to the Kordkuy road. Four thousand times, give or take.
I went on a Thursday morning and sat in the car park for forty minutes before I went in.

You know what the waiting room looks like. Everybody in this country knows what it looks like. Eleven women and two men, and of those, five with the tape across the bridge and the packing still in, and one of the men with it too, and the tape is white and it is meant to be discreet and it is the single least discreet object in the Islamic Republic, because everyone knows, and being known is at least half of what it is for. Girls wear it to weddings. Girls wear it who have not had the operation.
A television on the wall with the sound off. Plastic chairs in rows. A woman at the desk with a book.
And on the wall behind her, framed, in a good hand, the thing that made me put my hand on the back of a chair:
And He taught Adam the names, all of them.

That is the verse. It is a common enough verse; it is on a thousand walls. It is the verse about God teaching Adam the names of all things, and any Muslim in the world can have it on the wall of any business and it means nothing more than a pious decoration.

Except that in our books, and only in our books, that verse has one meaning and one only, and it has had that meaning since a merchant's son in this city wrote it down six hundred years ago: the names taught to Adam were the thirty-two letters. Not the names of animals. Not vocabulary. The alphabet, entire, handed over in advance of everything, in the first minute of the human world.
That verse, on that wall, in that waiting room, is a Hurufi sentence.

There is no possible way for it to be there by accident, and there is every possible way for it to be there by accident, and I stood in the door of a cosmetic surgery on the ring road of a provincial city and understood that I was not going to be able to tell the difference — not that day, not with what I had, maybe not ever — and that this had been the condition of my entire life and I had simply never before been in a room where it cost anything.
The woman at the desk asked if I had an appointment.
I said I wanted to see the doctor.
She asked what it was regarding, in the voice they use, the one that means consultation or complaint, and I heard myself say:
"Tell her Hormoz Rafi'i's student is here."
Hormoz [hor-MOZ] was my teacher's first name. In twenty-six years I had used it out loud perhaps four times, because you do not call your ostad by his name, alive or dead.
She put her pen down.

She did not ask me who Hormoz Rafi'i was. She did not ask me my name. She went through the door behind the desk, and she was gone four minutes, and when she came back she held the door open and said, "She will see you now," and thirteen people in plastic chairs watched me go in ahead of all of them.
PART TWELVE — THE RIGHT NOSTRIL
She was fifty-three and she had her father's hands.

That is the first thing I saw and it took the legs out from under me before either of us had spoken, because I had watched those hands for twenty-six years — the long flat thumb, the way the fingers sit slightly apart at rest instead of closing — and I had last seen them in a box eleven years ago being carried out of a house I have keys to.
"Sit down," she said. "You look like you are going to go over."

The room was a consulting room. A desk, two chairs, a lightbox on the wall with nothing on it, a sink. On the desk a photograph of two young men in a garden who I took to be her sons, and a paperweight, and a cup of tea that had gone cold enough to have a skin on it.
"You knew my father," she said.
"He taught me."
"Yes." She looked at me the way you look at a document. "You are the reader. You are Sanam's husband."
I had not told the woman at the desk my name.

I want to slow down here, because everything I had rehearsed in the car park for forty minutes went out of me in that first minute, and what happened instead was a conversation of about ninety minutes that I have gone over so many times since that I can no longer be certain which parts are memory and which are the smoothed thing you get from handling.
I am going to set it down as straight as I can.
"You have the verse on the wall," I said.
"Yes."
"And He taught Adam the names, all of them."
"Yes."
"Do you know what that verse means?"

"I know what it means to you," said Parvaneh Rafi'i [par-vaa-NEH ra-fee-EE]. "It means the names were the thirty-two letters. It means the whole alphabet was handed over in the first minute of the world."
"Anyone can have that verse on a wall."

"Anyone can." She turned the cold tea a half circle on the desk without picking it up. "It has been on that wall since 1961. My grandfather put it there. Are you going to ask me the question, or are we going to do this for an hour?"
So I asked her the question.
"How long has this clinic belonged to the lineage?"
And Parvaneh Rafi'i said: "Since my great-grandmother. I am the fourth."
What she told me, that morning, in the consulting room, with the door shut.

I am setting this down as a recitation because that is what it was. She spoke without stopping for a long time, in the cadence I have heard in a courtyard every year of my life, and when she had finished she drank the cold tea, which I found more frightening than anything she had said.
You have been reciting our history for six hundred years, she said, and you stop it in 1441.

Tabriz. The five hundred burned. The daughter with no grave. Then the crossing — the books going west into Anatolia, into the Balkans, into the dervish lodges in Albania where men who did not believe a word of it kept our papers on a shelf for five centuries because they had been asked to.
And then you say: six hundred years of nothing.
You say it every year. You said it last month; my cousin was there and told me. Six hundred years of nothing, and then here we are, three families in a provincial city.
It was not nothing. You simply were not told.
Think about what actually happened to us after Tabriz. Not the books. The people.

There were survivors in this province. Not many; enough. And they had learned in the hardest way available that a doctrine which announces itself gets its adherents burned in a square, and so they did what every hunted people does, and they went quiet, and they became fathers and grandmothers and men who sold cloth.
And they carried a doctrine which says — say it with me, you have said it all your life — that the human face is the writing of God.

Now. You are a hunted family holding that belief. You are living among people who would kill you for it. What is the one profession, of all the professions available in this world, that would let you spend your entire working life with your hands on the writing?
You have been reading faces. We have been keeping them.

Barbers, first. That is not a joke and I will not have you smile at it. My great-great-grandfather's father was a barber in the old bazaar and a barber in this country did everything — he shaved you, he took your teeth out, he set your arm, he lanced what needed lancing, and he did all of it on and around the face and nobody thought about it twice. Four generations of our men had the razor on the seven lines of half this city and no one ever asked them why they were so careful.

Then a surgeon, when there started to be surgeons. My great-grandmother. Trained in Tehran, came back here, opened two rooms above a shop in 1934 and did cleft lips and burns and the noses of men who had been hit in the face, and she was the only woman doing it in this province and they let her because there is work that men will not do on other men's wives.

Then my grandfather. Then my father — yes, your ostad, yes, the man who taught you, he was in this building three days a week for thirty years and you never once asked what he did on the days he was not teaching you, because a boy does not ask and a man does not think to start.
Then me.
And here is the part you came for, so sit still.
We do not consider what we do a violation of the writing.
We consider it copying.

You recite it yourself. Every year, on the twelfth night, you stand in that courtyard and you tell the children the one useful thing this doctrine has ever learned: we do not survive in bodies, we survive in copies. His daughter sat down and copied out her father's book with her own hand and then she burned and the copies did not.
You say that. You have never once asked what it obliges you to do.

She copied the Book of Eternity. Very well. What is the other scripture? What did your entire life's work consist of? The face is not like the writing, you say, it is the writing — you have said that in my father's house at my father's table, he told me, he thought it was the best thing you did.
Then every face in this city is a manuscript, and every one of them is unique, and every single one of them is going to die.
Nobody is copying them.

Six hundred years and it never occurred to any of you. You sit with the dying and you read them out loud, once, into a room, and then the page goes into the ground and the reading goes into a folder in somebody's house, and you call that preservation. It is not preservation. It is a description of a book that no longer exists. It is what a man writes on the outside of a burned crate.
We copy.

When a girl comes in here at seventeen and asks for a nose, she does not know what she is asking for and I do not tell her, and I never will, and you may despise me for it. She goes out with a face that reads cleanly. Her lines separate from the ground. Her brow stops arguing with her lash. She becomes, at seventeen, easy to read — and she will be read, at her funeral, by you or by whoever comes after you, and the reading will be better because of what happened in this room.
I have made four thousand faces legible in this province.
You have read perhaps four hundred.
Which of us has served the writing?
I said — and it took me a long time to get it out — "You have forged four thousand faces."
And she said the thing that I have not been able to put down for a year.
"Ostad Sarmadi. Tell me the test."
"What?"

"Tell me the test that distinguishes a forged line from a true one." She had her father's hands flat on the desk. "You are the finest reader this lineage has produced in a hundred years and you have been in this city for forty-eight of them. I have been cutting faces four streets from your house for thirty years and my father did it for thirty before me and his father before him. You have read our work. You have read hundreds of pieces of our work, at funerals, out loud, in front of families, and you have called it the writing of God.
"Not once. Not one time in your entire life have you looked at a face we made and said: this is false.
"So tell me the test. And if you cannot tell me the test, do not stand in my room and say the word forgery, because forgery is a claim about a difference, and you do not have one."
PART THIRTEEN — THE LEFT NOSTRIL
She showed me the books because I asked, and she showed me the books because she wanted to, and I have stopped trying to work out which of those was the larger part.

Not a computer. There is a computer, and there are the records the state requires, and those are downstairs and they are exactly what you would expect. What she took me up to was a room on the second floor with a window onto the car park, and shelving on three walls, and on the shelving the ledgers.
Ninety-one of them. Cloth spines, the older ones in a size they do not make any more.
"Nineteen twenty-eight to now," she said. "The barbers did not keep any. Or they did and we lost them. My great-grandmother started this the year she opened."
I took one off the shelf at random, the way you do, and it fell open the way old books do, and it was a page of a woman's face in 1954.
Here is what a page looks like, because I have not been able to stop describing it to people.
At the top, the date and a number. No name — I will come to the names.

Then a drawing of a face. Front, and both three-quarters. Not a good drawing; a working drawing, done fast, the outline barely there, because the outline is not the point. What is on the drawing is the seven, marked in — the scalp line traced, the two brows traced, the four lash lines traced, each one with a small measurement beside it in a hand I could read because it is the hand my teacher taught me to write in.
Then, underneath, a second drawing of the same face.
The proposed one.
The same seven lines, redrawn. And beside each of them, in the same hand, what it would then say. The letter. The value. The little marginal note about how it would sit against the ones around it.
They are readings. That is what stopped me on the stairs and made her put her hand on my arm.
Every page in that room is a reading — taken to the standard I was trained to, in the format my teacher taught me, with the light noted at the top of the page — of a face that did not exist yet.
They read the woman. Then they read the woman she would become. Then they cut, until the second reading was true.
"There are no names," I said.

"There are names." She took the book out of my hands and closed it and put it back in its place on the shelf, and she was careful about it, and that carefulness is the thing I think about most. "The names are in the index. The index is downstairs and it is mine and you are not going to see it."
"Parvaneh—"

"Four thousand women in this province," she said, "who do not know. Whose husbands do not know. Whose daughters do not know. You want the index so that you can look up one name, and I understand exactly which name, and I am telling you that the index does not open for one name. It opens for all of them or none."
"Then open it for one."
"No."
"She is my wife."
"She is four thousand people's wife," said Parvaneh Rafi'i.
I sat in the car in the car park for a long time.

I want to record what I actually thought about, because it was not the thing you would expect. I did not think about whether Sanam was in the index. I already knew Sanam was in the index; I had known it since the word threaded came out of a nineteen-year-old's mouth in my back room with the light going, and everything since then had been a man walking towards a fact he had already accepted in order to be able to say that he had checked.
What I thought about in the car was my own hand.

Because the drawings are in Ostad Rafi'i's hand. Not all of them — the older ones are his father's and his grandmother's, and there are perhaps fifteen years of them that are Parvaneh's, and hers is different, faster, more of a doctor's. But the middle of that room, three decades of it, is my teacher's handwriting.
And my handwriting is my teacher's handwriting.

He taught it to me the way you teach a child to hold a spoon, over years, correcting the angle of the pen with his thumb, and every reading I have ever entered into the lineage's archive is in that hand, and every proposed face in that room upstairs is in that hand, and if you took a page of mine and a page of his and put them side by side on a table, a stranger could not tell you which of us had served the writing and which of us had drawn a woman who did not exist yet.
That is not a metaphor about influence. I mean it literally. I mean that the archive of my religion and the order book of a cosmetic surgery are written in the same hand, and it is mine.
Sanam told me herself. I did not have to find it.

That is the part nobody believes when I say it, and I have stopped trying to make them believe it, because the version where a man uncovers his wife's secret is a story and the version where his wife puts it in front of him on a Thursday night is not a story, it is a marriage.

I had been home four hours. I had not said where I had been. She let me not say it through the meal and through the news and through the business of the tablets, which by then took eleven minutes and two glasses of water, and then she sat down opposite me at the kitchen table and put her hands flat on it, which was the thing she did before difficult sentences and had been for twenty-four years.
"You went to the Light Clinic," she said.
"Who told you?"
"Nobody told me. You have been to Kordkuy and back four hundred times and you have never once come home smelling of that soap." She let that sit. "Ask me."
"Ask you what."
"Mansur. Ask me."

I could not do it. I want that on the page. I sat in my own kitchen with my mouth open and could not put the question into it, and my wife watched me fail to and then took it off me, the way she had been taking things off me since we were young.

"I was nineteen," she said. "It was my mother's idea and I did not fight her about it, so it was also mine. My nose, here—" she put a finger on the bridge, on the good side, and ran it down "—and the brows, both, taken up at the ends, and the hairline lifted at the temples because I had my father's temples and I hated them.

"It was the summer before I met you. It was four months before. I healed for six weeks with tape on my face in my mother's house and then in the autumn two families sat down in a front room with a plate of sweets on the table and a young man read me and said I was a clean copy."
I said: "You knew what I was."
"Everyone knew what your family was. It is a small city."
"You knew what I would do for a living. You knew I would read faces. And you sat in that room and let me read—"
"Say the rest of it," said Sanam.
"—a face that had been made four months earlier."
"Yes."
"Why?"

And my wife said: "Because I was nineteen and a man who was going to be somebody looked at my face for two minutes and said it was clear. Do you know what that is, at nineteen? I did not think I was deceiving a priest. I thought I was pretty and it had worked."
We sat there.
The tap was going somewhere in the pipes the way it does in that house.
"When did you understand?" I said.

"That it mattered? Properly?" She thought about it. She was always honest about the dates. "Eight years in. There was a funeral in Aliabad and you read an old woman and afterwards in the car you said something about how you could always tell a face that had been helped — you used that word, helped — and how the letters go flat, how there is a deadness in them.
"And I sat in the passenger seat and I thought: he has read me every day for eight years.
"And then I thought: he cannot tell."

She said that last part without any triumph in it at all. That is what I cannot get past. There was no triumph in it. She had been carrying the single fact that would have taken my life's work apart, and she had carried it for sixteen more years, and what was in her voice when she finally put it down was tiredness.
"Why did you never say?"
"Mansur." She looked at me out of the face she had left. "What would you have done with it?"
I did not sleep. I went into the back room and put the lamp on and sat with my father's commentaries and did not open any of them.
Here is what I did instead, and it is the worst hour of the fourteen months.
I went through the readings.

Not hers. All of them. Twenty-six years, four hundred and eleven readings in the archive in my hand, and I sat in that room from midnight until the call to prayer and went through them in my head — every woman under fifty I had ever read, every clean copy, every face that had made me think this one is a pleasure, every time I had stood in a front room and told a family what God had written on their mother.
I could not clear a single one.
Not one. There is no reading in twenty-six years that I could pick up and say: this one, at least, this one was untouched.

And at some point in that hour it turned over in me, the way a thing does at four in the morning, and I stopped asking how many of them had been to a clinic and started asking the other question, which is the one I have not been able to put down since:
Would it have mattered?

Because I read those faces correctly. I read them by the discipline, in proper light, at the proper distance, and the sentences I said in those front rooms were true sentences about the lines that were in front of me, and the families wept, and some of them still telephone me at Nowruz.
If a made line reads, and a reader reads it, and the family is comforted, and the dead woman is buried under a sentence that a man drew in a room over a car park in 1987 — what, exactly, is missing?
I could not find it. I sat there until it got light and I could not find the missing thing, and that is when I understood that Parvaneh Rafi'i had not been defending herself in that consulting room.
She had been reciting.
PART FOURTEEN — THE TUFT
It was Parvaneh who told me, and she did not tell me kindly, and I have come to think that was correct.
She telephoned the house. That in itself frightened me — nobody telephones this house except about deaths — and she said, "Bring the photographs," and put the phone down.

I took the whole run. Fourteen months of them, every eleven days, in the folders, in two carrier bags, and I drove out to the ring road on a Tuesday morning in the fourteenth month with my wife's face on the passenger seat.

She cleared the desk with her forearm. Then she put them up on the lightbox in order, six at a time, and stood back, and we went through fourteen months of Sanam in about forty minutes without either of us saying very much.
Then she took down all but two.
The first frame and the last.
"Look at the nose," she said.
I had not looked at the nose in a year.

You have to understand why, and it is not stupidity, it is training. The nose is not one of the seven. In a woman there is nothing on the nose at all — the two nostril lines are paternal, they arrive with the beard, she never had them and never would. The nose is ground. It is the blank part of the page, the space the letters sit on, and a reader learns in his first year to look through it the way you look through the white of a page to the writing.
I had spent fourteen months reading the lines. The whole lineage had. There is not one sentence about her nose in the entire archive.
"Look at it," Parvaneh said again.
And I looked, and the nose in the first photograph and the nose in the last photograph were not the same nose.
The bridge in the early frame was straight and narrow and very slightly scooped, the shape you see on half the young women in this country and on none of their mothers. In the late frame it was not.
There was a small fullness in it, low down and to the right, and the tip had come down perhaps two millimetres, and there was a fractional widening at the base on the side where everything was going.
"That is the illness," I said. "It is taking that side."
"No."
"It is taking everything on that side."

"Mansur." She said my name and not my title, and I noticed it, and I think she meant me to. "The illness takes fat and muscle and bone. It thins. Everything it touches goes down and gets smaller." She put two fingers on the late frame. "That is bigger."
She explained it to me twice, because I did not take it the first time.
I am going to put it here the way she put it the second time, in the plainest words she had, standing at a lightbox with her hands behind her back.

When you make a nose smaller, she said, you do not take the nose off and put a smaller one on. You take pieces out. You take out cartilage — the springy stuff, not bone, the part you can bend between your fingers at the end of your own nose. You take some of it out and you rearrange what is left and you hold it in the new shape with stitches, and then the body heals around the new shape and calls it home.
But the body did not agree to it. The body is holding that shape the way a man holds a heavy suitcase: for as long as he is asked to, and not one minute longer.
Everything in that nose has been under tension for twenty-five years.

Now something comes along and thins the ground underneath the whole right side of her face. It takes the padding out from under the work. It softens what was holding, and the stitches are long gone, and the tension has nothing to pull against any more.
And the shape lets go.

Not fast. Over months. It does not spring back — nothing springs back after twenty-five years — it drifts, a little at a time, in the only direction it was ever going to drift, which is back towards the shape it was cut out of.
"Her face is not being destroyed," said Parvaneh Rafi'i. "It is being undone."
We stood there.

I want to describe what happened in me and I have never managed it properly. It was not a realisation. A realisation is a thing that arrives. This was more like a floor being taken out from under a floor.
Because if that was true of the nose, it was true of everything.

The brows. Both of them taken up at the ends, at nineteen, with a blade. That work sits in the same soft ground, held by the same tension, and the ground on the right had been thinning for fourteen months.
Her right brow had not dropped.
It had been let go of.

It had come down, over fourteen months, towards the place it had been in before a man in a room over a car park drew a second picture of a nineteen-year-old and then made the picture true. And I had sat on the floor of my bedroom in the fourth month with a lamp on a folded towel and read that motion and called it a descender — the stroke a scribe pulls down at the end of a word to say this closes here — and I had written in a notebook that it was the finest thing I had ever read.

And the hairline. Lifted at the temples, both sides, at nineteen, because she had her father's temples and hated them. Fourteen months of thinning ground underneath a lifted hairline. Of course it bowed. Of course it broke. It broke exactly where a blade had gone in twenty-five years earlier, and thirty adults argued for six weeks about what a broken line meant in the eyes of God, and not one of us — not one — asked why it had broken there.
Everything I had read as revelation was the sound of an old operation coming apart.
And then the second floor went, which is the one I actually live on now.
Because it does not follow that the readings were wrong.

Turn it over. Go slowly. For fourteen months I read a face that was moving, and everything I read on it was better than anything I had ever read on her — denser, stranger, more determined, arguing with itself. I did not invent that. Six other readers found the same and wrote it down independently in four houses in this province.
What was underneath the forgery was better than the forgery.

The face she was born with — the one a nineteen-year-old girl cried about for a year and a mother paid to have taken away, the one with her father's temples and a heavy nose and brows that sat where brows sit — that face was the finer text. It always was. It was under there the whole time, and the only thing that ever brought it back up into the light was an illness eating my wife alive.
I have not been able to decide, in the time since, which of these two sentences is true, and I have come to believe that the doctrine cannot decide either:
The disease is destroying the writing.
The disease is restoring it.
I asked her for the page.

Not the index. I had stopped wanting the index somewhere on the drive out, and I told her so, and I meant it. One page. The page with my wife on it, from the summer of the year we met, and I said I would not ask her for a name and I would not ask her for another sheet as long as I lived.
Parvaneh looked at me for a long time.

Then she went downstairs and was gone eleven minutes and came back up with a single leaf out of a ledger, cut out, which she had done with a blade in an office by herself rather than let me hold the book, and she put it face down on the desk and kept her hand on it.
"You understand what you are asking for."
"Yes."
"No," she said. "You understand what is on the front. You do not understand what is at the bottom." She took her hand away. "I am sorry. That is not a thing I have said in this building before."
The date was the fourth month of that year. Two months before I had ever heard her name.

The first drawing was a nineteen-year-old girl with heavy temples and a strong nose and level brows, and even in that fast working outline, even in three-quarter view with the ground barely indicated, I could read her. It was Sanam. It was Sanam more than the woman I married was Sanam, and I sat down without meaning to.
The second drawing was my wife.

I mean that flatly. The second drawing, the proposed one, the one with the seven lines redrawn and the little marginal notes about how each would sit against the ones around it — that was the face I had read across a plate of sweets in a front room in the autumn, and across a table for twenty-four years, and I knew every stroke of it the way you know a door in the dark.
And in the margin beside the second drawing, in the hand I write in, four words: clean. will read easily.
At the bottom of the page there is a line for the operator, and it is signed, because every page in that room is signed, because they are careful people and always have been.
H. Rafi'i.
I did not do anything for a while.
Then I did the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is the reason I have written this book, and it is very simple and anyone can do it.
The fourth month. He drew that face in the fourth month.

In the sixth month of that same year, Hormoz Rafi'i came to my father's house — I was twenty-four and I have the day itself, I have what I was wearing — and sat in the front room and told my parents that it was time I was married, and that there was a family in Anjirab with a daughter, and that he had heard she was a clean copy.
He had heard.

He had drawn it. He had drawn it eight weeks earlier in a room over a car park, on a nineteen-year-old girl who had cried at her mother for a year, and he had written will read easily in the margin in the handwriting he was at that time still correcting on me with his thumb.
And then he waited eight weeks for the swelling to go down, and then he went to my father's house.
I have tried, for a year, to find another reading of that page. I want to put the alternatives down because I owe it to a dead man who loved me.
Perhaps it is coincidence. Four thousand women. In a city this size he would have cut half the young women I might have married; the odds of a page are not the odds of a plot.
Perhaps will read easily is a professional note and nothing more. It is what he wrote on hundreds of pages. It means the work will heal clean.
Perhaps he thought he was doing a kindness twice over — a girl made happy, a student given a wife whose face would not fight him.
Perhaps.

But I keep coming back to a thing that is not evidence and that I cannot get rid of, which is that in twenty-six years that man never once told me he had a daughter who was a surgeon, or that he worked in a building on the ring road, or that our doctrine had a second half.
He taught me to read.
He did not teach me that there was writing in the world that had been done by a hand like mine.

And I have sat in four hundred and eleven front rooms and told four hundred and eleven families what God had written on the faces of their dead, in a hand I learned from him, in a city he had been quietly editing since before I was born.

I went back one more time, to say the thing I had driven out there to say, and she let me say all of it.
I said: he made her.
I said: your father made my wife, eight weeks before he came to my father's house, and wrote in the margin that she would read easily, and then handed her to a boy he was teaching to read.
I said a number of things after that which I am not going to put down, and Parvaneh Rafi'i sat behind her desk and took them, and did not once tell me to lower my voice, which I was not lowering.
When I had finished she said: "Sit down."
I sat down.
"Now I am going to give you the only comfort available," she said, "and you are not going to like it, and it is still the only one."
And she recited to me, from memory, in a consulting room, the passage from the Book of Eternity about the four letters.

She did it properly. She did it the way it is done in a courtyard, in the cadence, without hurrying, and she is not a reader and has never stood up in front of the lineage in her life, and she had it word for word, which told me who had taught it to her and when.

Four letters, she said. Pe, che, zhe, gaf. Made by men. Made in a workshop, out of letters that already existed, by putting dots on them, eight hundred years after the revelation closed, because a Persian mouth makes four sounds an Arab mouth does not and the scribes needed to write their own language down.
Everyone knows this. It is not hidden. It is not a scandal. It is in any book on the alphabet.

And the man from this city, who saw the glory in Tabriz in the fasting month and had his head taken off for it twenty years later, wrote that those four letters are pre-eternal. That they were among the names given to Adam in the first minute of the world. That the scribes who thought they were inventing were remembering, and that their hands were being run, and that a letter added by a man in good faith and a letter written by God are the same letter and no instrument in creation can separate them.

"That is your doctrine," she said. "Not mine. Yours. It is the load-bearing wall of the whole house. Take it out and the thirty-two collapses into twenty-eight and the fourteen collapses and the seven collapses and your entire lineage is a family of men who look at hair.
"So you may have one of two things.

"You may have a doctrine in which what my family has done for four generations is scripture — in which case your teacher wrote your wife the way God wrote the four letters, and you have been reading his hand and God's hand and they are the same hand and there is no crime because there is no difference.

"Or you may have a test. You may have some way of telling the true line from the made one. And on the day you produce it, you will have proved that four letters of the Persian alphabet are counterfeit, and the thirty-two is a lie, and everything your people have believed since 1374 goes into the fire with it.
"You cannot have your outrage and your doctrine. They are the same wall."
She let me sit with it.

Then she said, more quietly: "I have known this since I was fifteen. My father sat me down in this room and gave it to me exactly as I have given it to you, and I want you to understand that he was not being clever. He was frightened. It was the only thing he had that let him keep doing this and keep believing, and he handed it to me because he could not carry it by himself any more."
"He did not hand it to me."

"No," said Parvaneh. "He gave you the reading. He kept the cutting. I have thought about that my whole life and the kindest thing I can make of it is that he wanted one person in this lineage who could still look at a face and simply believe it."

Golnaz asked me to read her.

It was three weeks after the page. The visits had thinned — I do not know why, and I have a theory I will not write down — and the house was quiet again for the first time in a year, and she came on a Tuesday and we sat in the back room under the north window and she said it as though she had been carrying it up the path.
"I want you to read me. Properly. For the archive."
"No."
"Ostad—"
"No."
"Why?"

And I said, because I was tired and because I had stopped being careful: "Because I would be reading a page that a family of surgeons wrote on you when you were seventeen, and putting it into the archive of this lineage in my teacher's handwriting, and calling it the word of God."
Golnaz did not say anything for a while.
Then she said: "Sanam is in the back bedroom."
"I know where my wife is."

"You have read Sanam nine times in the dark and once a week for a year in front of strangers, and you have just told me that a face like mine is not fit to go in the book." She was not crying. I would have preferred it if she had been. "Say what you mean. Say it properly and I will go."

And there was nothing available to me, because she was correct, and because a man who will read one made face and not another is not making a judgement about scripture. He is making a judgement about which women he can bear to be wrong about.
So I read her.

I did it badly — I want that recorded, because it was the last reading I have taken and it was the worst work of my life. I could not hold the discipline. I kept seeing where the ends of the brows had been lifted, which I had never once seen in eleven previous readings of the same girl and which I could not now stop seeing, and twice I lost the ground entirely and had to go back to the top of the page.
It took four hours. It should have taken ninety minutes.
At the end I gave her the sentence, and it was thin, and she wrote it down in her own hand and thanked me and put her shoes on in the hall.
At the door she said: "You have taught me for nearly two years."
"Yes."
"You have never once asked me what I think it says."
"What do you think it says?"
"Not now," said Golnaz Ehsani. "I am going to be the one who reads you, one day, and I would like to come to it clean."
31 — ZHE
Here is where it stands, and I am going to set it out flatly, because I have discovered that the flat version is the only one I can look at.

The hollowing is finishing. That is not hope and it is not a doctor being kind; it burns out, in most people, after some years, and everyone who has looked at her since the autumn says the same thing in the same careful voice. It is slowing. It will stop. It has taken what it is going to take.
Which means that in some month, without any announcement, my wife's face will be finished.
Not healed. Finished, the way a book is finished. Four lines and a fragment, held in whatever arrangement it has arrived at, and no more writing.
And on that day there are two things I may do, and they are both obedience, and I have been sitting with them since the spring.
The first is to do nothing.

Let it stand. Let the undoing be complete. Let the temples she was born with come back and the brows sit where her mother's sat and the nose be her father's nose, and hold that what has happened is a restoration — that a girl was forged at nineteen by a man in a room over a car park, and that God has spent fourteen months patiently rubbing it out, and that the face at the end of this is the one that was issued to her.
It is a good reading. It is defensible on every page of our books. It also requires me to say, out loud, to my wife, that the thing that ruined her life was a correction.
The second is to telephone Parvaneh Rafi'i.

Because it can be helped. Not undone — nothing is undone — but there are things that can be put back under the ground on that side, and a brow that has let go can be lifted again, and a woman who cannot close her eye can be given an eyelid that closes, and my wife has not slept a full night without tape on her face in fourteen months.

The books permit it. That is the part I did not expect and it took me a long time to find. The old ruling that curses the ones who alter what God has made — the plucked brow, the filed tooth — has a clause on the end of it that nobody quotes, and the clause says: except in the treatment of disease. It is not beautification if it is repair. Every scholar in every school agrees on that and has for a thousand years.
So I would not even be sinning. I would be permitted, in writing, by everyone.

And I would be sitting in a chair in that clinic while a Rafi'i cut my wife's face into a shape that I chose, in the room where her father cut it into a shape he chose, and I would be the second man in her life to draw a second picture of her.
There is no third thing. I have looked for a year.

And the doctrine will not help me, because the doctrine is not neutral between them — it is enthusiastic about both. It says the writing is living and continuous, so the illness is authorship. It says a letter added by a man in good faith cannot be told from a letter written by God, so the surgery is authorship.
Whatever I do, I am obeying.
That is the answer I was given. I asked for six hundred years and I was answered by all of it at once, and the answer was: yes.
32 — GAF
She sits in the chair under the north window in the afternoons because the light is good and because it is habit now, and neither of us has moved it back.
Yesterday there was a low sun coming in under the cloud, the way it does here in the winter for about twenty minutes before it goes, and the whole room went the colour of weak tea.

I had the telephone in my hand. I had had it in my hand for most of an hour. The number is on a card in my wallet and it has been in my wallet since the Thursday of the photographs, and I have taken it out perhaps two hundred times, and it is soft at the corners now the way card goes.

She had her eyes shut. Not asleep. She does that in the afternoons, sits with them shut and her hands in her lap, and I used to think she was resting and she told me once that she is simply having the only twenty minutes of the day in which nobody is looking at her face, and that I could stay if I did not talk.
I stayed. I did not talk.
Then, without opening her eyes, my wife said:
"What does it say today?"
And there it is. That is the whole thing. That is what I have been walking towards since a girl put her hands under her thighs in this room and told me where she got her nose.
Because she is asking for a reading. She has asked me for one every day since the autumn, and I have given her one every day since the autumn, and there is not one of them that has been the truth.

I could tell her what is on her face. Four lines and a fragment, arguing, and every one of them in the middle of coming apart from an operation in 1987, and the finest text I have ever read in my life, and none of it hers, or all of it hers, depending on a question that no instrument in creation can settle.
I could tell her that a man I loved drew her on a Tuesday in the fourth month and wrote in the margin that she would read easily.
I could tell her nothing, and pick up the telephone.

Or I could do the thing she asked me for in the dark in the ninth month, in the kitchen, with the light off — say one thing that is not on my face — and I have had two years to find it, and I have found it, and I have not said it yet, and I do not know whether I am going to.
The sun was going. It goes fast here.
My wife sat in the chair with her eyes shut and her hands in her lap and waited, the way she has waited for twenty-four years, and I put the telephone down on the arm of the chair.
And I opened my mouth.
GLOSSARY

alif [a-LEEF] Arabic/Persian, first letter of the alphabet. A single vertical stroke, undecorated, with the counting value of one. It stands for unity and for the beginning of the alphabet, and it is the mark a scribe makes first when testing a new pen.
Alinja [a-leen-JAA] place name, Nakhchivan. The mountain fortress where Fazlallah Astarabadi was beheaded in 1394 on the order of
Miranshah. His grave there became a place of pilgrimage, circled seven times and then seven times again.

ana'l-Haqq [a-nal-HAQQ] Arabic, ‘I am the Truth’. The declaration of the Sufi martyr Hallaj, executed in Baghdad for it in 922. Nesimi took it into his verse, and it is arguably what he was flayed for rather than the doctrine of letters.

Astarabad [as-taa-raa-BAAD] Persian, the old name of Gorgan. The north-eastern Iranian city where Fazlallah Astarabadi was born. The name fell out of use in the twentieth century, which is why few people connect the founder of Hurufism with the modern town.
Darmangah-e Nur [dar-maan-GAAH-eh NOOR] Persian, ‘the Light
Clinic’. The cosmetic surgery on the ring road in this novella. Invented.
dervish [DER-vish] Persian darvish, a poor man. A member of a Sufi order; in the older sense, a wandering ascetic who owns one bag, keeps no house, and is fed by strangers.
Fatiha [FAA-teh-heh] Arabic, ‘the opening’. The first chapter of the
Qur'an, seven verses long. Hurufi doctrine reads its seven against the seven maternal lines of the face.
Fazlallah Astarabadi [fazl-ol-LAAH as-taa-raa-baa-DEE] Arabic/Persian,
‘the generosity of God’. Founder of Hurufism, c. 1340–1394. A merchant's son and celebrated interpreter of dreams before his vision in
Tabriz. Author of the Book of Eternity. Beheaded at Alinja.

Firishteoglu [fee-rish-teh-OH-loo] Turkish, ‘son of the angel’. The scholar who rendered the Hurufi doctrine into Turkish some sixty years after Fazlallah's death, and by whose version much of it survived.
Gilan [gee-LAAN] place name, northern Iran. Caspian province of Iran.
Gorgan [gor-GAAN] place name, north-eastern Iran. The modern city built where Astarabad stood. The setting of this novella.
Haji Sorkh [haa-JEE SORKH] Persian, ‘the red pilgrim’. Leader of the
Hurufi rising in Isfahan in 1431, in which two sons of the governor were killed. Taken alive and skinned.
Hallaj [hal-LAAJ] Arabic, ‘the wool-carder’. Mansur al-Hallaj, the Sufi executed in Baghdad in 922 for declaring ana'l-Haqq. An early influence on Fazlallah.
he-ye do-cheshm [heh-yeh do-CHESHM] Persian, ‘ha with two eyes’.

The Persian name for a form of the letter ha, so called because in the flowing nasta'liq hand it resembles a pair of eyes. A genuine teaching device of calligraphers, and a small gift to letter-mystics.
Hormoz [hor-MOZ] Persian given name. The first name of Ostad Rafi'i.
Hurufi [hoo-ROO-fee] Arabic huruf, letters. An adherent of the doctrine that God is the twenty-eight and thirty-two letters, and that the human face is not like scripture but is scripture.

istiva, khatt-e [khat-teh es-tee-VAA] Arabic istawa, ‘he settled’. The line of settling: the vertical axis down the centre of the face, from hairline to chin. Not one of the fourteen letters but the place from which they are read — taken from the Qur'anic verse that God settled upon the throne, which Fazlallah read as the throne of Adam's form.
Javdan-nama [jaa-vee-DAAN naa-MEH] Persian, ‘the Book of Eternity’.
Fazlallah's chief work, written in the dialect of his own province and preserved because his daughter copied it out by hand.

Kaaba [KAA-beh] Arabic, ‘the cube’. The black cube at Mecca which every Muslim faces in prayer. Hurufi doctrine read it as the face and head of Adam, the sevenfold circumambulation standing for the maternal lines and the second seven for the paternal.

Kalimat-Allah al-‘Ulya [ka-lee-MAT-ol-laah al-OL-yaa] Arabic, ‘the highest word of God’. The name taken by Fazlallah's daughter, who preserved his book by copying it and who was burned with some five hundred others at Tabriz in 1441.
Karbala [kar-ba-LAA] place name, Iraq. Where the grandson of the
Prophet was killed in 680; a place of pilgrimage for Shi'a Muslims.
Khorasan [kho-raa-SAAN] place name, eastern Iran. Province with an early Hurufi following.
khutut-e abiya [kho-TOOT-eh a-BEE-yeh] Arabic/Persian, ‘the paternal lines’. The seven lines of the face that arrive at puberty and descend from
Adam: the hair down each side of the face, the two halves of the moustache, the hair in each nostril, and the tuft between the lower lip and the chin. Women do not receive them.

khutut-e ummiya [kho-TOOT-eh om-MEE-yeh] Arabic/Persian, ‘the maternal lines’. The seven lines present from birth in every human being, descending from Eve: the hairline, the two eyebrows, and the four sets of eyelashes.
Kordkuy [kord-KOO-ee] place name, Golestan province. A town west of
Gorgan.

Miranshah [mee-raan-SHAAH] Persian, ‘prince-king’. Son of Timur and governor of Azerbaijan, who ordered Fazlallah's execution and who was, by most accounts including his family's, going mad in those years.
Nakhchivan [nakh-chee-VAAN] place name, South Caucasus. The mountainous region containing Alinja.
nasta'liq [nas-taa-LEEGH] Persian, a calligraphic hand. The flowing, hanging script in which most Persian literary manuscripts are written.
Naubar [now-BAR] place name, Tabriz. A quarter of the city of Tabriz.
Nesimi [neh-see-MEE] pen name, Arabic nasim, breeze. The greatest
Hurufi poet, who met Fazlallah once. Flayed alive at Aleppo early in the fifteenth century. Tradition holds that he went on reciting.
ostad [os-TAAD] Persian, master, teacher. The man who taught you your trade and to whom you never stop owing it. You do not call him by his name, alive or dead.
pe, che, zhe, gaf [PEH, CHEH, ZHEH, GAAF] the four Persian letters.
The four letters Persian has and Arabic does not — the sounds in pedar

(father), chesm (eye), muzhde (good news) and gol (flower). Scribes built them centuries after the revelation closed by adding dots to existing letters. Hurufi doctrine holds them nonetheless to be pre-eternal, among the names taught to Adam — and therefore that a letter added by a human hand cannot be distinguished from one written by God.
Sarmadi [sar-maa-DEE] Arabic sarmad, everlasting. Family name.
Shirvan [sheer-VAAN] place name, South Caucasus. Region with an early Hurufi following.
Tabriz [tab-REEZ] place name, north-western Iran. Where Fazlallah received the manifestation of glory in 1374, and where some five hundred
Hurufis were burned in 1441.
Timur [tee-MOOR] Turkic, ‘iron’. The conqueror known in Europe as
Tamerlane. Fazlallah attempted to convert him.
zuhur-e kebriya [zo-HOOR-eh keb-ree-YAA] Arabic/Persian, ‘the manifestation of glory’. Fazlallah's name for what happened to him in
Tabriz in the fasting month of 1374. He never described the event, only what he was given by it.
